articles.title: Investigation into Powerhouse Parramatta museum under way as stop-gap leader steps in
articles.summary: ‘Opera House of the west’ still slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November, NSW arts minister says

blocks.text: An investigation is under way into allegations of misconduct involving senior executives at the soon-to-be-opened Powerhouse Parramatta.
The $915m museum in western Sydney, billed as one of the world’s most significant new museum projects, is set to open in November.
On Thursday, Powerhouse chief executive Lisa Havilah stood aside, pending the investigation of fresh allegations regarding governance and procurement at the museum, the NSW government announced.

Allegations had been put to several Powerhouse executives as part of a misconduct investigation ahead of the institution’s formal opening, NSW arts minister John Graham confirmed at a budget estimates hearing on Monday.

“The idea that two of the senior executives were working through this process, this detailed process, and could also make sure that went smoothly was really starting to become unsustainable,” he said.
The museum’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave and is providing significant information as part of the investigation, Graham said.
Havilah agreed to step aside following a conversation about further allegations that had come to light, the department of creative industries secretary, Melanie Hawyes, told the hearing.
But she cautioned any interim leadership arrangement should not be interpreted as a sanction or finding.
“These allegations that have come to light need to be tested, and that is what this investigation will do,” said Hawyes.

NSW government architect Abbie Galvin has been appointed interim chief executive and former Opera House chief executive Louise Herron has been appointed as a strategic advisor, with both to start their roles on Tuesday.
A separate NSW Treasury review of the museum’s operational budget is separate to any allegations, Hawyes said.

Spending at the Powerhouse under Havilah’s leadership has included items such as a documentary on the building of the institution, to cost at least $1.7m, about $5m on marketing, and $333,500 on the interior design of on-site accommodation.

In response to a whistleblower complaint, an initial probe was launched in March 2025 and the state’s anti-corruption commission was notified, while a formal misconduct investigation began last December.
The procurement deals in question were under about $6m, the amount the chief executive is authorised to spend without ministerial approval, the hearing was told.
Graham defended his handling of the controversial project, insisting that issues going back to at least 2023 had been dealt with appropriately.
The Powerhouse board members including chair of trustees David Borger were not subject to the the allegations, and the board’s audit committee has assisted with investigations, Graham confirmed.
The minister said he was confident the project, which he described as the Opera House of the west, would open to the public as scheduled on 7 November.

articles.title: Search begins for Canadian team to restore uninhabitable 24 Sussex Drive
articles.summary: The search is officially on for a Canadian team to renovate Canada's most famous fixer-upper — 24 Sussex Drive — so it's no longer uninhabitable and future prime ministers can once again live there.

image.caption: A new procurement document calls for Canadian companies to put their names forward to take part in a competition to redesign and rebuild the prime minister's official residence at 24 Sussex Drive that is currently uninhabitable. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The search is officially on for a Canadian team to renovate Canada's most famous fixer-upper — 24 Sussex Drive — so it's no longer uninhabitable and future prime ministers can once again live there.
Canadian materials, Indigenous participation required to restore prime minister's official residence
The federal government recently posted its first procurement notice for the long-awaited rehabilitation project, which opens the door for domestic companies to pitch themselves as contenders.

The document reveals that Ottawa will choose seven finalists during this first stage to move on to the national design competition, with the winning team awarded a design and construction contract by the fall of 2027.

Ottawa is looking for a "world-class design vision" that focuses on using Canadian products to transform the gutted official residence into a secure and modern home and place to work for future prime ministers, the document said.
"Given its national and historical significance, the rehabilitated residence must be completed by Canadians for Canadians," the Request for Qualification (RFQ) posted on Aug. 21 said.
"In that spirit, the use of Canadian materials and innovations must be considered and incorporated throughout the project."
Carney wants 24 Sussex fixed up for future prime ministers

The official residence has sat vacant for more than a decade. Successive prime ministers have been unwilling to take the political risk to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on renovations, allowing the building to deteriorate. In recent years, the heritage home had to be stripped down to the studs to remove asbestos, mould and dead rodents.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called the state of the official residence an "embarrassment" in an exclusive interview with CBC News earlier this year. He unveiled his long-awaited plans in June to restore the heritage home built for his successors through a national design competition and a fundraising campaign to help foot the bill.
Canadians have donated more than $735,000 as of late July — almost 1.5 per cent of the $50 million fundraising goal.
Details of competition
The government's new RFQ is the first stage of the procurement process. The nearly 100-page document provides the most detail in writing about the competition to date.

Teams pitching a design plan must show they can create a private living quarter for the prime minister and their family while balancing space for work, meetings, hosting receptions or ceremonial events, the request said.
The winning team, according to the document, will also be responsible for making the property universally accessible, handling landscaping elements and restoring heritage elements.
The main building has already been gutted to remove "hazardous materials," the document said, but there might be archaeological assessments, geotechnical studies and security-related modifications.

The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada will use a jury of experts to score the design concepts, and a separate technical evaluation board at Procurement Canada will judge the construction plans, budgets and schedule, the request said.
The RFQ is a way for the government to screen potential teams and weed out any that aren't qualified.
The teams who want to compete must show they have experience working on a series of projects including a complex building that cost at least $50 million to build.
Carney launches design competition to 'rehabilitate' 24 Sussex Drive
The procurement rules also make it mandatory that competing firms' plans include Indigenous people and businesses to carry out at least five per cent of the contract's total value.
It's still unclear how much it will cost to renovate the famous property.
The construction budget is expected to be included in the next phase of the procurement process, known as the Request for Proposal, expected to launch in the winter of 2027, the request said.

items: Carney confronts our national home reno nightmare at 24 Sussex

blocks.text: The top contenders will ultimately compete to showcase designs that "inspire pride" and "architectural excellence," according to the rules.
"The desired outcome is a renewed 24 Sussex [that] serves contemporary needs and remains a symbol of Canada for generations to come," the request said.
The Rideau Hall Foundation, which is leading the fundraising effort for the project, said it's planning on a more formal launch of its campaign in the coming weeks.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ashley Burke is a senior reporter with the CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa. She was recognized with the Charles Lynch Award and was a finalist for the Michener Award for her exclusive reporting on the toxic workplace at Rideau Hall. She has also uncovered allegations of sexual misconduct in the Canadian military. You can reach her confidentially by email: ashley.burke@cbc.ca

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial Day 20: AFP official to testify on DepEd funds
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – As Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, the House prosecution panel will present Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Col. Manaros Boransing II…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – As Vice President Sara Duterte’s trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, the House prosecution panel will present Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Col. Manaros Boransing II on the Department of Education’s (DepEd) confidential funds.

According to the prosecution, Boransing will testify on whether or not the AFP received financial assistance or monetary rewards from DepEd for the annual Youth Leadership Summit (YSL) when Duterte was the education secretary.
When the Commission on Audit questioned DepEd use of P112.5 million in confidential funds in 2023, DepEd submitted certifications from military officers to explain its expenditures.

However, during the 2024 House committee on good government and public accountability hearing into DepEd’s secret funds, military officers testified that their units did not receive DepEd intelligence funds for the annual summit.
It was at this forum where Boransing testified they would not have issued the YSL certification had they known that it would be used by DepEd to justify its fund expenditures.

Testifying after Boransing is AFP officer Col. Magtangol Panopio, who also testified during the House hearing two years ago.Panopio is anticipated to speak to corroborate Boransing’s testimonies on the military certifications. /mr

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial (September 1, 2026)
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte continues on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. Here are the latest news and updates.

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 7:24am
The Senate impeachment court in session for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Senate/File photo
Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 20: What to expect

A new witness is set to be presented by the House prosecution panel on Tuesday, September 1, in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, this time coming from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).

The prosecution will call to the witness stand retired Colonel Manaros Boransing II to testify on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Duterte of committing impeachable offenses due to systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds.

To recall, in October 2024, lawyer Michael Poa told the House good government and public accountability panel that he asked then-Department of Education (DepEd) undersecretary and retired Major General Nolasco Mempin to request certifications from military units to back up the department's spending of the P15 million in confidential funds for informants in 2023.
The Senate impeachment court has also issued a revised subpoena for Colonel Magtangol Panopio. His testimony will come after Boransing.

Boransing and Panopio were among the military officials who previously said that they issued military certifications, but maintained they were not aware that these were used to liquidate the DepEd's confidential funds.

On Friday, House prosecution panel adviser and former Surigao del Norte Representative Ace Barbers and House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said that the military certifications issued by Boransing and Panopio to justify DepEd's confidential fund spending carry great weight because, aside from these being public funds, it is not the job of the military to liquidate these confidential fund disbursements of DepEd.

The prosecution team also said that Poa, then-undersecretary and spokesperson of the DepEd, has a lot to explain before the Senate impeachment court on how the P112.5 million in confidential funds of the DepEd was used during the tenure of Duterte as Education chief. —Giselle Ombay/LDF/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Health-care groups call on Ottawa to stop Alberta’s dual medical practice model
articles.summary: Canadian and provincial health-care groups are calling on the federal government to stop Alberta from allowing physicians to practise in both the public and private system.

image.caption: Jason MacLean, chair of the Canadian Health Coalition, called on federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel to stop Alberta from allowing physicians to practise in both the public and private systems. (CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Canadian and provincial health-care groups are calling on the federal government to stop Alberta from allowing physicians to practise in both the public and private system.
Alberta gets nearly 400 expressions of interest from physicians
· CBC News
· Posted: Aug 31, 2026 7:09 PM EDT | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago
The change is enabled by the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 (No. 2), commonly called Bill 11, which takes effect on Tuesday.

“[Bill 11 is] the biggest threat against health care since the Canada Health Act was passed in 1984,” Jason MacLean, chair of the Canadian Health Coalition, said at a news conference in Ottawa Monday.

The group is planning rallies in 30 locations across Canada on its so-called Day of Action on Tuesday. The rallies will be followed by 50 town halls this fall as part of its national campaign against the bill.

MacLean said he believes changes enabled by the bill will make access to health care unequal. He said when physicians are able to practise in both systems, resources tend to migrate towards the private pay system, creating long waitlists in the public system.
MacLean called on federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel to take action before other provinces follow suit.
“We don't understand why the federal government is mute on this. This is an issue of national consequence,” he said.
“We all know what happens in Alberta won't just stay in Alberta.”

items: Federal health minister voices concern as Alberta implements dual-practice health-care model

blocks.text: Bill 11 was introduced and passed in Alberta’s legislature in the fall 2025 sitting, allowing doctors to apply to be able to practise in both the public and private spheres.

In order to be eligible to apply for dual practice in Alberta, physicians need to work a prescribed number of hours in the public system. Family physicians are not allowed to practise in both systems at this time.

According to the province, surgeries under the dual-practice model likely won’t start until later in the fall because physicians must get approved by the government first. They can start applying in mid-September.

Maddison McKee, press secretary for Alberta’s Hospital and Surgical Health Services Minister Adriana LaGrange, told CBC News that the province is reviewing nearly 400 expressions of interest received from physicians about the new dual-practice option over the summer.
“This will help us gauge interest, understand what specialists are contemplating dual practice and prepare for the formal application process,” she wrote.
“Applications will be reviewed to ensure eligibility criteria and government requirements are met, including public surgery hour requirements, monitoring and new reporting requirements.”
Province insists dual practice is allowed

McKee dismissed concerns raised by the Canadian Health Coalition about what it sees as Alberta moving to a U.S.-style health-care system as “fearmongering.” She said dual practice doesn’t violate the Canada Health Act.

“Our priority is a strong public system and ensuring Albertans never have to pay out of pocket for medically necessary care — which is a commitment we have made under our Public Health Care Guarantee,” she wrote.
“Expanding access through dual practice does not take away from that. It adds to it. This is not an either/or debate. It is about giving Albertans more choice.”

Earlier this month, Michel told the Toronto Star she was concerned about Bill 11. On Monday, her spokesperson, Alexandre Bergeron, said the federal government was collaborating with Alberta on any changes “that respects their jurisdiction to explore innovative ways to improve access and care while strengthening the public, universal health-care system.”
“Minister Michel is advancing targeted discussions with her counterpart focused on ensuring access to medically necessary care and the core principles of the public system are protected,” he wrote.
“A collaborative approach between our governments has always produced strong results for all Albertans and we will continue to work in that direction.”

items: Eligible doctors in Alberta can work in both public, private systems starting this fall

blocks.text: The federal government sent a letter to the province on July 24 confirming it had reviewed the regulations and the June 18 ministerial order, and that both levels of government should continue their collaboration.

Bergeron said Ottawa is in close contact with the province to ensure possible adverse impacts on the public system are mitigated and that changes are in compliance with the principles of the Canada Health Act.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michelle Bellefontaine covers the Alberta legislature for CBC News in Edmonton. She has also worked as a reporter in the Maritimes and in northern Canada.

articles.title: Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say
articles.summary:
Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’

The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the…

blocks.text: The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.

UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.
With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.

Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”

Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused on plastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.

Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.

Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”

She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping board.”

Submissions of evidence to the report showed particular concerns around the presence of microplastics in soil, which Bowyer said “impacts the biological, the chemical and the physical functioning of the soil and the soil fertility itself”.

According to Bowyer, plastic particles affect the soil structure, changing the water capacity of soil; they affect the microbial community, the bacteria and fungi that are crucial to soil health; and they affect the soil fauna, with earthworms ingesting microplastics undergoing physiological changes.

She said it was important to remember that “soil is not an inert material. It’s a complex living ecosystem; it’s very finely balanced. [It is a] complex ecosystem that supports the growth of crops that feed us. The second thing to remember that’s really important is that microplastics, they’re not just polymer particles … they’re basically chemical cocktails.”
There are more than 16,000 chemicals used in plastics. About 4,000 are known to be harmful to health, while most of the rest have never undergone safety testing, the report notes.
after newsletter promotion

“Microplastics can also pick up from the environment further contaminants,” Bowyer said. “So they become like sponges or magnets for other things like bacteria, heavy metals, viral particles, other chemicals.”

The report makes five policy recommendations: legally binding targets for cutting microplastic pollution, regulation of the largest sources of microplastic releases, extended producer responsibility to reduce releases across the plastics lifecycle, improved wastewater, sewage sludge and soil protections, and a coordinated national monitoring and evidence system to oversee the issue.

The report’s co-author Dr Antaya March, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute’s Global Plastics Policy Centre, said: “The UK has an opportunity to move from a fragmented response to a coordinated strategy that tackles microplastics across the plastics lifecycle. We should not wait for every scientific uncertainty to be resolved before acting where the evidence already shows that intervention can prevent pollution and reduce future risks.”
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs was contacted for comment.

articles.title: UK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research reveals
articles.summary:
Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years

A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average,…

blocks.text: A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees.

The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found.
The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the Good Schools Guide.

However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school.

The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors.
Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area.
Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas.

In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288.
after newsletter promotion

However, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243.

Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.”

Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%.
Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198.

Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole.

articles.title: Pilandok won’t directly affect PH but habagat to prevail
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Depression Pilandok will not directly affect the country, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over Luzon and the western part of Visayas…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Depression Pilandok will not directly affect the country, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over Luzon and the western part of Visayas on Tuesday, according to the state weather bureau.

In the 5 a.m. weather forecast of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration, weather specialist Veronica Torres said that Pilandok was last estimated 1,050 kilometers east of Extreme Northern Luzon. It maintained its strength as it was carrying a maximum wind speed of 55 kilometers per hour (kph) and gustiness of 70 kph.
“Walang direktang epekto sa ating bansa at napakababa naman ng tyansang maglandfall sa anumang parte ng bansa,” Torres said.
(This does not have a direct effect over the country and it has a low chance of making landfall in any part of the country.)

Torres also said that Pilandok will move east-northeastward and then northeastward in the next 24 hours. It may also traverse northwestward and exit the Philippine area of responsibility by Wednesday evening or Thursday morning.
It is forecast to intensify into a tropical storm in the next 12 hours.

Meanwhile, Torres noted that the habagat will bring heavy rains in the western portion of Luzon. She added that Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Batanes, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan will experience 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall on Tuesday due to habagat.
Weather disturbances outside the country
Torres also shared that there are currently three weather disturbances being monitored outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR.

Tropical Storm Saudel, formerly locally named Obet, was last located 965 kilometers west of Extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 a.m. Torres said that because of its east-southeast movement, its chance of re-entering the PAR is not ruled out.
A tropical depression seen 645 kilometers west-northwest of Itbayat, Batanes is not forecast to enter the PAR.

Lastly, a low pressure area 3,000 kilometers east of Southern Luzon has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression in the next 24 hours. Its possibility of entering the PAR is not ruled out. /jpv

articles.title: Cardinal David: Resilience not acceptance of corruption, incompetence
articles.summary: "There comes a point when resilience becomes dangerous because it teaches us merely to endure."

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 7:00am
Motorists commute through a flooded street due to rains brought by the southwest monsoon in Pampanga on August 31, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Filipino resilience should not mean passive acceptance of corruption, incompetence and neglect, Kalookan Bishop Pablo Virgilio Cardinal David said Monday as floods continued to disrupt communities across Luzon.
In a social media post on Monday, August 31, David urged Filipinos to go beyond enduring disasters and instead demand accountability for preventable suffering.
"There comes a point when resilience becomes dangerous because it teaches us merely to endure," David said.

"After every disaster, we are told to be resilient. This time, let us also be defiant... Let us refuse to normalize preventable suffering. Let us demand answers. Let us demand accountability. And where the law allows it, let us act together as citizens to hold accountable those who fail in their duty to protect the public," he added.
David said such defiance should take the form of organized, legal civic action rather than simply anger on social media.

He encouraged motorists to file complaints before regulatory agencies, communities to demand disclosure of flood-control projects and budgets, and citizens to seek legal remedies when negligence results in injury or loss.

"Defiance asks questions: Who designed this? Who built it? Who inspected it? Who maintained it? How much did taxpayers pay for it? Why does the same place flood every year? Where did the flood-control money go?" David said.
"And when negligence is established, who will be held accountable?"
David cited recurring flooding along the North Luzon Expressway in San Simon, Pampanga, where he said he was recently trapped in traffic for almost five hours.
Flooding continued to disrupt traffic in the San Simon area Monday, with some NLEX lanes impassable to smaller vehicles.

Parts of Bulacan also remained flooded after days of southwest monsoon, or habagat, rains. Floodwaters remained inside historic Barasoain Church in Malolos earlier Monday before receding later in the afternoon.
"Filipino resilience is a beautiful virtue. But resilience should never mean passive acceptance of incompetence, corruption or neglect," David said.

articles.title: Q&A: Canadian man held in ICE detention centres for 9 months shares challenges while detained
articles.summary: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained. Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most…

image.caption: Curtis Wright, centre, his fiancée Kayla Thomsen and their daughter are pictured in this undated handout photo. Wright was recently returned back to Canada from the U.S. on a removal order after being detained by ICE for the past nine months. (Kayla Thomsen/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained.

Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most of his life living in the United States, was held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas for nine months after returning from a business trip to Mexico in November.
Wright said the reason he was detained stems from a misdemeanor drug possession charge from when he was 17 years old.
Wright said he was motivated to fight to remain in the U.S to try to be with his two young sons from a previous marriage, aged 8 and 11, who are in Texas.
Wright said he was returned to Canada in mid-August, and is temporarily staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna, B.C., with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.
In an interview with Edmonton AM on Monday, Wright detailed the challenges he faced while struggling to remain south of the border.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
LISTEN | Curtis Wright ends up back in Canada after months in ICE detention:
Edmonton AM10:57Edmonton born Curtis Wright is back in Canada after nine months in ICE detention centres in the U.S.
What happened when you returned to Texas after a work trip to Mexico?
When I was going through Immigration and Customs, they asked me to go into secondary screening, which isn't uncommon. I've been through that before, but this began pretty differently.
He right away asked me, “Were you charged with misdemeanor possession back in 2004?”
I said “Yes, I was.”
He said, “OK, make a text to one of your family members. Let them know that this is going to be a while because we're going to have to investigate this further.”
Once I did that, they brought me into a back interview room where I was interrogated almost as if I were on trial, like I had done something wrong at that moment.

Then once the interview was over, he said, “As of this moment, you're now being detained. You'll be taken to a federal facility, and you won't have a court date until Dec. 3rd.” And this was on Nov. 6.

From that point, they moved me to a separate room and then from there they shackled me, put the waist chains around me, handcuffed me to my waist, put on ankle shackles, as if I was some kind of murder convict, and had me wait in a cell then took me to the facility.

items: 12 international students at Calgary protest referred to CBSA office after status check
On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional

blocks.text: Has anything like this ever happened to you previous to this encounter?

Never. I've gone in and out of the U.S. probably over 100 times since this has happened. I came to Kelowna to visit my parents at their home just this last summer just a few months before this detainment.
I was under the impression that they were focusing on the worst of the worst, like gang members, and people of that nature. I didn't realize that they were going to be detaining me.

items: Canadian man stuck in ICE detention centre for 4 months, awaiting deportation hearing

blocks.text: What options did they give you about what could happen next?
Really nothing. The guy informed me that because I was being federally detained there's no bond available to me because they marked me as a visiting alien reentering the country.
I was told later that if ICE had grabbed me in the country, I would have been able to get a bond potentially so I could fight my case outside.
But they purposely marked me as a visiting alien so that I couldn't get a bond. And then he said, “You're just going to have to go through the court case.” So that's essentially what I did.
Then that took this whole nine-month process to go through that court case?
They keep pushing your court case back because the whole idea behind it is they want you to give up. They don't want you to fight your case.

They put you in these horrible facilities and treat you very, very poorly, and they continue to push your court cases back. So you think you're going to court and then they say, “No, actually it's going to be in another three weeks. Oh wait, no, it's going to be in another two weeks.” Because they want you to give up and just go home.

items: Canadian who was held in ICE facility for months back in detention despite judge's ruling rights were violated

blocks.text: How many times did that happen to you where they pushed it?
For my first court date, it happened four times. I was originally scheduled to have it on Dec. 3 but didn't end up having it until Jan. 16.
After about five months, I finally went through the court case process and lost.

You’re supposed to get three dates and your third date is your trial date where a judge renders a decision. But I didn’t even get the opportunity to fight my case. On my second court date, they just said “Order of removal.”

Then I appealed after that and we tried to get a federal release through a writ of habeas corpus. The whole idea behind that was to get out so I could fight outside, and then we'd continue to do continuances and continuances and continuances waiting for the next political regime or hopefully winning my appeal. But I was never given the opportunity to do that.

items: How the U.S. secures its northern border
Canada's immigration 180: Part 1

blocks.text: You were fighting to be released back into Texas. That's where you called home. I understand that's where some of your family is as well?
The main reason that I was fighting to stay in Texas is because I have two sons with a previous wife.
I knew if I went to Canada they wouldn't be able to come with me. At the time I had 50/50 possession, so I got them half the year.
I fought because I wanted to stay in my children's lives as much as I possibly could, so that's why I stayed for nine months until we exhausted every option.

We had Republican senators write in asking for my release. We had Democrat senators write in asking for my release. We had Texas state representatives, even one individual who was on the board of commissions for Texas State prisons and detention centres, he wrote to ICE, the federal courts, the immigration courts. They all did.

Then I fought my case and we tried federal release. We went to the media. I exhausted every option because, to me, it was important to leave with no regrets, knowing that I did everything I could to stay with my boys. And that one day when I have to tell them why Dad had to leave, I can tell them with honesty that, “Your father did everything he possibly could.” But it just didn't work out.

items: How Trump’s mass deportation plan became big business

blocks.text: Can you tell us about what you experienced over those nine months in those centres?

It's the hygiene side of it. There's dirt, mould and grime everywhere. Everything's run down. I mean, you're sharing a small bathroom and showers with 100 men. There are a hundred men in the dorms. The food is just abysmal.

But more than that, it’s the officers that are there in place to be security for you. They yell at you. They curse at you. They threaten you. Solitary confinement is always one of their biggest threats, or moving you to different dorms or taking away privileges.

The lights are on 24 hours a day. You're sleeping in a steel bunk bed with no pillow. You're asked to be counted in your bed five times a day, and it's almost like a psychological and emotional beatdown.

Because, as I mentioned before, they want to make things as uncomfortable as they possibly can for you because they want you to give up and just go back to your home country. You feel like you're less than human.

items: How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

blocks.text: When did you finally decide to be deported to Canada?
I finally made that decision about eight months in, and then it took about another month to get out.

Because my lawyer had informed me that in the federal courts there's an ongoing case right now pertaining to permanent residence and due process, and that the judge that had my habeas corpus for a federal release was waiting on the ruling of that case, and it had already been ongoing for several months.

The lawyer said the case “could go on for two more weeks or it could go on for two more years. So, you could wait another year, year and a half, let’s say, and then the ruling goes against permanent residents. And then you can’t get release on that anyways.”

items: Canada's immigration 180: Part 2

blocks.text: At that point, I realized it was just the best thing for my family because even though I'm the one locked up in there, my whole family's going through it. I feel like we were all stuck in this terrible, terrible nightmare.
I thought it was important for the whole family that we just kind of move on and find a way to just move forward with our lives the best way we can and accept what is, and so that's what we're doing.
But again, I love Canada and there was no concern about coming back here. It was simply trying to stay there for my sons.
What are your next steps from here?

My career has been in oil and gas and so, being from Edmonton, it's kind of a perfect spot to pick that right back up. Thankfully, my company that I was working for before in Houston, is going to be opening up a Canadian division just for me to run and try to grow here in Canada.

I've had a lot of wonderful people in my corner, including my employer, and they're going to continue to stick by me and most of my family is in Edmonton — all my aunts, uncles, cousins, my brother and his wife and children are there.
