articles.title: The 1st Fat Marmot Week winner is a 'special boy who likes to eat rocks'
articles.summary: Dawn, fuzzy fat father who likes the taste of rocks, is officially the most popular yellow-bellied marmot in Gothic, Colo. The Fat Marmot Week contest is the brainchild of the Marmot Project, a…

image.caption: Dawn is the winner of the year's Fat Marmot Week contest by the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory's Marmot Project. (Movements/Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory)

blocks.text: As It Happens

Dawn, fuzzy fat father who likes the taste of rocks, is officially the most popular yellow-bellied marmot in Gothic, Colo. The Fat Marmot Week contest is the brainchild of the Marmot Project, a long-term research initiative whose future hangs in the balance amid U.S. funding cuts.
Contest is the brainchild of The Marmot Project, a research project facing critical funding cuts
LISTEN | Interview with Fat Marmot Week organizer Katie Adler:
As It Happens5:52The 1st Fat Marmot Week winner is a 'special boy who likes to eat rocks'
A fuzzy fat father who likes the taste of rocks is officially the most popular yellow-bellied marmot in Gothic, Colo.

When the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory held its inaugural Fat Marmot Week this summer, the contest was twofold — a popular vote, and a weigh-in to see which contestant packed on the most pounds ahead of hibernation season.
Dawn won both.

According to his online bio, he is known for fathering several litters of baby marmots, and licking the salt and minerals off of rocks. He nearly doubled his body weight this summer from 3.8 to 5.9 kilograms, or roughly 5.5 to 13 pounds.
"He definitely deserved it," Fat Marmot Week organizer Katie Adler told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal. "He is a special boy who likes to eat rocks."

But heavy is the head that wears the crown. As champion chonker, Dawn has also taken on the unofficial role of ambassador for the Marmot Project, a long-term research program whose future hangs in the balance amid widespread science and education funding cuts in the U.S.
Funding cuts could kill 60-year research project
Fat Marmot Week is inspired by Fat Bear Week, a popular contest run by Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.
Like bears, marmots are hibernators, and soon, Gothic's population of yellow-bellied marmots will tuck themselves away for an eight-week winter rest.
"They have to put on all that weight so that they don't freeze over the winter," Adler said. "So they get absolutely huge."

Adler, a graduate student in ecology at the University of California, Los Angeles, works for the Marmot Project, a long-term generational study of yellow-bellied marmots out of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Colorado.
Launched in 1962, it is the world's second longest-running study of individually marked mammals, after Jane Goodall's famous chimpanzee research in Tanzania.
Over the last six decades, its researchers have studied 5,000 marmots over 12 generations, says University of Ottawa biologist Julien Martin, one of the Marmot Project's leaders.
"From a human perspective, it would be kind of going back, in terms of generations, to the beginning of the 1700s," Martin said.

"In parallel, we are also tracking the environment. So what we're doing is we're trying to understand how, essentially, the wild animal of nature is adapting and evolving with the changes in the climate and all the perturbations that humans are bringing."

items: Trump budget cuts funding for clean air and water programs
U.S. science funding uncertainty reshapes grad school choices for Canadians

blocks.text: But the Marmot Project is on shaky ground.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has issued major cuts to research organizations, including a 20 per cent cut to the National Science Foundation (NSF), a major source of research grants in the U.S.
As a result, the NSF is expected to issue 30 per cent fewer new research grants this fiscal year, according to the journalistic arm of the journal Nature.
"The pot of money is shrinking, and there's more people applying to it," Martin said.
What's more, he says, cuts to higher education have made it difficult for research labs like the Rocky Mountain to remain properly staffed.
"It's a U.S.-wide problem of, essentially, the erosion of the structure needed for higher education," Martin said.
Turning to OnlyFans
That's why the Marmot Project has been spearheading outside-the-box public campaigns to raise awareness about their research and solicit donations.

Earlier this year, the Marmot Project launched OnlyMarms, an uncharacteristically family-friendly account on the usually sexually explicit platform OnlyFans, where subscribers can watch the critters on camera traps.
"We really rely on those long-term funding grants to propel this research forward," Adler said. "We have to think of other options, or this project might not be able to continue."
This G-rated OnlyFans page is all about marmots
Thanks to these efforts, the lab has managed to raise more than $120,000 US in donations.
"It's definitely going to help, and we're going to try to stretch the money for as long as we can," Martin said.
Still, he says, it's not a sustainable way to fund long-term research.
So the Marmot Project has launched a petition on Movements.mov calling on Congress in the U.S. to claw back its cuts to research.
Called "Don't Let American Science Depend on OnlyFans," it had 180 signatures as of Monday afternoon.
CBC has reached out to Democratic and Republican leaders in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, but did not receive any responses before deadline.
The Marmot Project, meanwhile, will continue doing what it can, including planning its next Fat Marmot Week for 2027.
Adler hopes campaigns like this help the public appreciate marmots as much as she does.
During her time in Colorado, she says she's watched them survive the heat and predators of summer while packing on enough pounds to make it through long, harsh winters.
"Marmots are resilient," she said. "I think I've gained a lot more respect for them, and I hope the public has, too."
Interviews with Katie Adler produced by Emma Marshall and Leslie Amminson

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 20: What to expect
articles.summary: The prosecution will call to the witness stand retired Colonel Manaros Boransing II to testify on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Vice President Sara Duterte of committing…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 6:09am

A new witness is set to be presented by the House prosecution panel on Tuesday, September 1, in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, this time coming from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).

The prosecution will call to the witness stand retired Colonel Manaros Boransing II to testify on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Duterte of committing impeachable offenses due to systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds.

To recall, in October 2024, lawyer Michael Poa told the House good government and public accountability panel that he asked then-Department of Education (DepEd) undersecretary and retired Major General Nolasco Mempin to request certifications from military units to back up the department's spending of the P15 million in confidential funds for informants in 2023.
The Senate impeachment court has also issued a revised subpoena for Colonel Magtangol Panopio. His testimony will come after Boransing.

Boransing and Panopio were among the military officials who previously said that they issued military certifications, but maintained they were not aware that these were used to liquidate the DepEd's confidential funds.

On Friday, House prosecution panel adviser and former Surigao del Norte Representative Ace Barbers and House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said that the military certifications issued by Boransing and Panopio to justify DepEd's confidential fund spending carry great weight because, aside from these being public funds, it is not the job of the military to liquidate these confidential fund disbursements of DepEd.

The prosecution team also said that Poa, then-undersecretary and spokesperson of the DepEd, has a lot to explain before the Senate impeachment court on how the P112.5 million in confidential funds of the DepEd was used during the tenure of Duterte as Education chief. —LDF/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
articles.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.

blocks.text: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.
If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.
Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.

Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.
It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.
MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.
Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.
Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.

More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.

"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200mn fund in India, told the BBC.
At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.

"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."
Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.
Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.

After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.
But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.

At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments through some 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. And Goyal has said , externalJapan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.
Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.

Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.

The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".

But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.

India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.

"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."
For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.

India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.
But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.

"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external.
"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."
Also, India remains a tough country to do business.
Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.

An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external.
Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.

It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

articles.title: Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo
articles.summary: Wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed part of the natural habitat of hundreds of orangutans, risking the survival of the species.

blocks.text: A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island.
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands.
The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species.
"The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water".
The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.

articles.title: Poa faces questions on P112.5-M DepEd secret funds
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson could emerge as a pivotal witness when the Senate impeachment trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, as prosecutors turn to the paper…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson could emerge as a pivotal witness when the Senate impeachment trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, as prosecutors turn to the paper trail behind the alleged misuse of P112.5 million in confidential funds at the Department of Education (DepEd).

Michael Poa, now also one of Duterte’s defense lawyers, is expected to face questions about military certifications he helped obtain for DepEd, where Duterte served as secretary for two years until June 2024.

Poa will be called to the witness stand after retired Col. Manaros Boransing II and Col. Magtangol Panopio, who are expected to shed light on certifications cited by DepEd in responding to Commission on Audit (COA) findings.
House prosecution adviser Robert Ace Barbers said prosecutors would examine certifications used to justify fund releases, including those tied to youth summits organized by DepEd.
Why Poa matters
The House prosecution team views Poa, who also served as an undersecretary and chief of staff at DepEd, as crucial because he figured in the agency’s response to the audit findings.
During a 2024 House inquiry, DepEd Undersecretary Nolasco Mempin testified that Poa requested military certifications for the agency’s response to a COA audit observation memorandum.
Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V described Poa as a “central figure” in the impeachment case, saying the Senate proceedings could clarify his earlier statements.

“His statements to the good government [committee] when he was a resource person are still incomplete … Now we are in the impeachment court and I believe this is the proper forum to clarify the questions,” Ortega said in Filipino.
Poa said last week he was ready to testify and did not intend to invoke attorney-client privilege unless necessary. Ortega said prosecutors were prepared for whatever Poa might say or invoke.

“He is the mouth of the Vice President and you cannot speak, you cannot defend, you cannot honor your words if you don’t know … all the details and you don’t know the whole process. That’s how important he is to the trial,” Ortega said.
Poa’s testimony could help establish who sought the military certifications, why they were obtained and how they were used to support the release and liquidation of confidential funds.
Fajarda sidelined
The prosecution’s original witness for the DepEd transactions, special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda, will not testify Tuesday after suffering a stroke. His appearance has been reset to Sept. 7.
Fajarda was supposed to testify on his role in disbursing and liquidating P112.5 million in confidential funds from the first to third quarters of 2023. /cb

articles.title: Lacson: P3.7B ‘wasted’ in Taguig reclamation
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — At least P3.713 billion in public funds may have been wasted on flood control and multipurpose projects in reclamation areas of Laguna Lake in Taguig City, according to Sen.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — At least P3.713 billion in public funds may have been wasted on flood control and multipurpose projects in reclamation areas of Laguna Lake in Taguig City, according to Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson.

Also on Monday, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano welcomed the scrutiny of land titles in his bailiwick, noting that his wife, Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, had long wanted these properties examined.

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has ordered a halt to reclamation projects in Taguig, saying it would soon “determine a way forward” on this matter after consulting with “different stakeholders.”

Posting on X on Monday, Lacson said: “WASTED PUBLIC FUNDS DUE TO MISUSE: Based on official records and our investigation, the total cost of Identified completed, ongoing (and suspended) DPWH Flood Control and Multi-Purpose Projects along the ‘illegal’ Laguna Lakeshore Reclamation Areas in Taguig City has so far reached P3.713 billion.”

“These do not include other anomalous Slope Protection and Flood Mitigation projects along Taguig River involving double appropriations and ‘ghost’ projects using recycled photographs in different ‘completed’ projects, for billing purposes,” he added.

Lacson’s latest disclosure came following Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon’s announcement of cease-and-desist orders issued on the said projects, in line with a directive from the Office of the President through the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA).
Lacson said earlier that an investigation by his team has found reclamation activities on Taguig City’s side of Laguna Lake covering at least 85 hectares of land.
He said their latest findings would be among the evidence to be sent to the Office of the Ombudsman’s fact-finding team “for proper disposition.”
Contractors
In his post on X, Lacson also cited official records as well as his office’s investigation identifying the top five contractors involved in projects covering P2.372 billion:
1) Dahl Construction: P858.22 million covering five solo projects worth P571.5 million and four joint ventures totaling P286.7 million;
2) JC Uyecio: P483.1 million covering four joint ventures;
3) ToughBuilt: P434.2 million covering three solo projects;
4) Topnotch: P329.9 million covering two joint ventures with Core Check and one with Beam Team; and
5) GR Fervidal: P266.6 million covering five solo multipurpose building projects
Lacson said all of the multipurpose building projects of GR Fervidal were suspended due to a “revision of plans” involving soil reinvestigation.
He said the DPWH issued the cease-and-desist orders “to prevent further waste of government funds on contractors carrying out unauthorized or illegal activities.”

Lacson also said earlier he was told by PRA officials that all unpermitted reclaimed areas in Taguig City, whether belonging to the local government or to private individuals, are subject to forfeiture in favor of the national government.

On Saturday, he disclosed that at least four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City had been initially identified as covered by “fraudulently” issued land titles, while at least four other parcels have no plotted title lots in the digital file of the Land Registration Authority (LRA).
‘Digging further’
In a statement on Monday, Cayetano said the government stands to gain if allegations of illegally titled properties along Laguna Lake in Taguig are proven true.

“Yesterday, there was something in the newspaper saying that there is a 181,000-square-meter, or 18-hectare, property that was supposedly ‘illegally titled.’ On one hand, we are also hoping that’s true. Why? Because if it is indeed illegal, it would go to the government. Then we would have 18 hectares now for the government,” said Cayetano, referring to one of the parcels identified by Lacson.
In another post on X, Lacson reacted to that statement by Cayetano.

“Maybe so, except that those titles (38.83 hectares total, so far) are registered to private individuals. We have their names as well as the OCT (original certificate of title) and TCT (transfer certificate of title) numbers. We are digging further deep into it,” said Lacson.
“What if it wasn’t exposed?” he added. /cb

articles.title: 2027 budget vulnerable to politicking, watchdog warns
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.2-trillion national government budget for 2027 is vulnerable to political manipulation ahead of the 2028 elections, with budget watchdogs warning that billions…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.2-trillion national government budget for 2027 is vulnerable to political manipulation ahead of the 2028 elections, with budget watchdogs warning that billions of pesos in discretionary and localized projects could be used for patronage despite shrinking fiscal space.
Kenneth Abante, coconvener of the People’s Budget Coalition, said the national expenditure program was not “people-centered,” as the Marcos administration claims, but “more centered on politicians.”
“We are worried that the 2027 budget will be politicized for the coming elections,” Abante told the Inquirer in a text message.
He said about P735 billion in discretionary funds could be exposed to “waste, fraud, abuse and patronage.”

Among the programs flagged as susceptible to political meddling are the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s cash assistance, the Department of Labor and Employment’s program for displaced workers, and the Department of Health’s medical aid for indigent patients.

Also at risk are infrastructure programs such as farm-to-market roads, health facility improvements and flood control projects.“It is striking that hyper-local, patronage-driven projects are prioritized,” said public finance specialist Zy-Za Nadine Suzara.

The Department of Budget and Management submitted the record spending plan to Congress on Aug. 11, a 6-percent or P407-billion increase from this year. The administration has described it as focused on education, health, food and social protection.

But a Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department document shows substantial cuts in several agencies under these sectors. Education faces a P39.2-billion reduction; health, P33.6 billion; social welfare, P28.7 billion; agriculture, P13.5 billion; and labor, P9 billion.

“It’s hard to characterize the 2027 proposed budget as a people-centered budget when funds for human capital development, livelihood support, agricultural productivity and commuter-centered transport programs suffered deep cuts,” Suzara said.
P107.4B for flood control

The Department of Public Works and Highways gets P113.1 billion more and the Department of Transportation P160.3 billion more. Debt interest payments rise by P164.3 billion and the National Tax Allotment by P129.3 billion.
The budget also sets aside P107.4 billion for flood control, a major corruption flashpoint.
Suzara said debt servicing, local government shares and government operating costs consume about 84 percent of the budget, leaving only P1.15 trillion in “real funding space.”
Blockchain budgeting

Amid the concerns, Sen. Bam Aquino renewed his call for passage of the Citizen Access and Disclosure of Expenditures for National Accountability (Cadena) Act, or Senate Bill No. 1506, the blockchain the budget bill.
The Senate approved the measure in December 2025, but it remains pending in the House.

The bill would require agencies to upload contracts, project costs, bills of materials and procurement records to a public Digital Budget Platform, making records accessible, tamper-resistant, traceable and verifiable. Officials who fail to disclose required documents or submit fraudulent information could face penalties.

Aquino said Cadena had fallen to 41st from third among the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council’s (Ledac) priorities. Socioeconomic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said he would raise the issue with Ledac leadership.
“The best way to address corruption is to have full transparency,” Aquino said, arguing that putting budget records on blockchain could help prevent misuse of public funds.
He said the measure was especially urgent amid renewed scrutiny of flood control spending and alleged misuse of public funds. /cb

articles.title: Flood control projects fail Central Luzon folk
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Flood control measures in Central Luzon region, including an ongoing river dredging program for the past seven years and the construction of flood control…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Flood control measures in Central Luzon region, including an ongoing river dredging program for the past seven years and the construction of flood control structures along major waterways, have proved ineffective in the past days against flooding caused by the enhanced southwest monsoon or “habagat.”
Thousands of families were again forced to evacuate as the death toll in the region from the effects of the monsoon rose to 31 as of Monday, with most of the fatalities from Zambales and Bulacan.
In Zambales, the dredging of Bucao River in Botolan and Sto. Tomas River in the San Felipe-San Narciso area has been among the flood mitigation efforts being conducted by the provincial government.

Department of Environment and Natural Resources Administrative Order No. 13 also identifies dredging along the Bucao, Maloma and Sto. Tomas rivers as a measure to restore heavily silted channels and help prevent flooding.
All these dredging activities, however, proved to be ineffective as floodwaters submerged communities in Botolan and further wrecked flood control structures already damaged by previous floods.
Damage estimate
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has so far reported P569.27 million in damage to flood control projects in Zambales, with P1.28 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction.

The DPWH 1st District in Zambales accounted for P472.42 million in damage, including sections of Bucao River Dike 7 in Barangay San Juan, Botolan, where more than 3 kilometers of slope protection were reportedly destroyed.
The DPWH 2nd District, on the other hand, recorded another P96.85 million in damage, including revetments along the Tamayok and Matain rivers in Subic and the Sto. Tomas River in San Marcelino.

blocks.caption: DESTROYED A section of Bucao River Dike at Barangay San Juan in Botolan, Zambales, is among the flood control structures reported destroyed in the latest assessment of the Department of Public Works and Highways. —Photo courtesy of Botolan LGU

blocks.text: The Zambales Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office reported that 710 families, or 14,052 people, had so far been evacuated. Of these, 552 families or 10,242 people were in evacuation centers as of Aug. 30.
Botolan recorded the highest number of evacuees in shelters with 3,491 people, followed by Cabangan with 1,938.

Agricultural damage and losses, on the other hand, reached P37.55 million, according to the Office of the Provincial Agriculturist. Rice accounted for P21.58 million, affecting 1,069.42 hectares and 1,267 farmers.
A state of calamity was earlier declared in Zambales following widespread flooding and damage from successive days of heavy rains.
‘Ground zero’
In Bulacan, the so-called “ground zero” of the flood control controversy, at least 15 people have died and three others injured since Aug. 10 amid heavy rains and widespread flooding.
The province also remains under a state of calamity with all 23 towns and cities affected by floods as high as 1.8 meters (6 feet) in some areas.

Fed up with the situation, at least 34 people’s organizations staged an anticorruption rally in Bulacan on Monday, demanding an end to reclamation projects and calling for accountability among officials linked to the flood control scandal.
The groups, under the banner of Kilos Bulacan, also called for comprehensive environmental and flood control measures, compensation for flood victims and stronger action on climate change.
The protesters first gathered at Malolos City Hall Amphitheater and near MacArthur Highway before proceeding to the provincial capitol to hold a short program.
Kilos Bulacan leader Obet Rodrigo said many of Bulacan’s rivers remain swollen, while Leonides Laderas of Hagonoy said the Aug. 31 rally was only the first in a series of planned street protests.
Heavy traffic on NLEx

In Pampanga, motorists traveling on the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) on Sunday were stuck in traffic for hours because of floodwaters ranging from knee to waist-deep in the San Simon and Tulaoc areas.
“Five hours hardly moving, with nowhere to go and no way to get off the expressway,” Kalookan Bishop Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David said of his “miserable” experience in a Facebook post on Monday.
Ironically, the Tulaoc overpass bridge had been raised by 0.7 meter three years ago to help prevent flooding in the area. It was also the first time the San Simon Interchange ended up under water.

The flooded portions along NLEx resulted in a long line of vehicles stretching about 8 km on the northbound side and roughly 6 km on the southbound side, NLEx Corp. assistant vice president for traffic operations Robin Ignacio said in a television interview.

For David, the ordeal was particularly “frustrating” because flooding in San Simon was hardly a surprise while NLEx Corp., which had access to real time traffic information, knew which sections were flood-prone.
“We pay substantial toll fees precisely because we expect a toll expressway to provide a reasonably safe, properly maintained and efficiently managed facility,” he said.
Monthlong death toll
Successive tropical cyclones, combined with the enhanced habagat, have caused widespread flooding in many parts of the country since Aug. 1, leaving 33 dead.
The Office of Civil Defense said on Monday that it is verifying reports about 14 additional fatalities.

Eleven of the fatalities are still under verification, supposedly drowned—nine in San Marcelino, Zambales; and one each in Olongapo City and Capas town in Tarlac. The remaining three were killed in landslides—two in Zambales and the third in Porac, Pampanga. OCD Assistant Secretary Raffy Alejandro IV said that four other individuals were missing after the collapse of the Agana Bridge in Tarlac City. This was on top of the three previously reported.

The death toll of 33 was reported earlier in the day by OCD Director Vicente Gregorio Tomas in a press briefing. He said that 19 others had suffered injuries, while the monsoon has so far affected a total of 8.8 million people nationwide.—WITH REPORTS FROM JOHN ERIC MENDOZA, AND JUN MALIG

articles.title: Built for floods: VinFast VF 6 has an IP67-rated powertrain
articles.summary: Techies might be familiar with the IP67-rating. It is typically a badge of honor for phones and action cameras, denoting their rugged and weather-proof design. Few cars can boast of a similar rating,…

blocks.text: Drive
The only car with an IP67 rating
Techies might be familiar with the IP67-rating. It is typically a badge of honor for phones and action cameras, denoting their rugged and weather-proof design.

Few cars can boast of a similar rating, save maybe for VinFast. The VinFast VF 6 is one of the few vehicles with an IP67-rated powertrain. This engineering design makes the VF 6 a weather-ready crossover, designed to withstand different roads and severe monsoon conditions in the country.

An IP67-rated powertrain can withstand dust exposure and water submersion for up to 30 minutes. Addressing one concern among prospective EV buyers in the country. The VF 6 features the said battery pack with a 59.6 kWh capacity, indicating protection against dust ingress and temporary water immersion. This ensures that no dust can enter the critical components of the VF 6, keeping its internal hardware safe from tiny debris and sudden floods. Likewise, the rating adds another layer of protection for the vehicle’s battery system, giving drivers peace of mind that their crossover remains safe in heavy rains, splashes, and spills during rainy season driving.

This weather-ready engineering answers the severe unpredictability of the Philippines’ rainy season. According to PAGASA, the enhanced Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) this August brought rainfall exceeding 200% of normal monthly averages. The MMDA also recorded 138 millimeters of rains in just two hours on August 17 – rates that mirrored 2009’s Tropical Storm Ondoy – triggering immediate flash floods across major thoroughfares. These downpours compound Metro Manila’s chronic gridlock, where the 2025 TomTom Traffic Index recorded a 57% congestion level and average speeds of just 18.9 km/h.

Rainy season gridlocks can turn a usual one-hour drive into a four-hour standstill – a scenario where traditional gas vehicles continue consuming fuel while idling. The VinFast VF 6, meanwhile, uses an electric powertrain that does not require the engine to idle while stationary. With over 450-km of NEDC-rated range and DC fast charging from 10% to 70% in 35 minutes, the VF 6 also offers the range and charging flexibility needed to fit into demanding daily routines.
Engineered for wet-weather conditions

Eager to address one of the major hesitations in EV adoption in the country, the VinFast VF 6 leverages its 170 mm ground clearance to navigate through urban flash floods. Its 1,650 kg curb weight provides the grounded physical footprint needed to maintain traction on pooled water. To keep the vehicle planted on slick surfaces, the Electronic Stability Program and Traction Control work alongside Electronic Brakeforce Distribution to help maintain stability and braking control when road conditions become unpredictable. Furthermore, Heated Side Mirrors and Defoggers help maintain clear sightlines when heavy rain and moisture compromise the driver’s view.

To reduce the mental strain of navigating busy, rain-soaked roads where torrential downpours blur lane markings and reduce visibility, the VinFast VF 6 is equipped with key Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) features. These include Adaptive Cruise Control, that maintains a safe distance from the vehicle ahead, helping reduce the need for constant speed adjustments in slower-moving traffic. Meanwhile, the 360-degree camera makes it easier to navigate tight streets and parking spaces by giving drivers a bird’s-eye view of their immediate surroundings. Blind Spot Detection and Rear Cross Traffic Alert add another layer of awareness. These features can be particularly useful in congested conditions, where reduced visibility and heavy traffic can make it more difficult to monitor vehicles approaching from different directions.
This is especially timely, given the MMDA recorded 23,260 road crashes in Metro Manila from January to May 2025 alone, underscoring the need for technology that supports driver awareness and safety.
For passive safety, the VF 6 Plus also comes equipped with eight airbags, while the Eco features four, providing additional protection for occupants in the event of a collision.
A mobility investment built for the rainy season

blocks.caption: Evoto

blocks.text: Evoto

The VF 6’s electric powertrain delivers 310-Nm of torque with responsive and controlled acceleration, helping drivers manage the frequent starts and stops of congested city traffic. When sudden rains conceal sharp potholes beneath standing floodwaters, the crossover’s rear multi-link suspension – a setup typical for higher-segment SUVs – helps provide a more composed ride over uneven roads.

Ownership is further protected by a seven-year or 160,000-km vehicle warranty and a 10-year or 200,000-km battery warranty, delivering vital long-term protection against the harsh wear-and-tear of the rainy season. VinFast also offers free unlimited charging at V-Green stations until March 31,2029, alongside complimentary accessories like a home wall charger with installation.

Priced at P1,699,000 (battery included) and P1,409,000 (battery subscription), the VinFast VF 6 fuses weather-ready engineering with intelligent driver assistance and comprehensive ownership support. Whether you are navigating rain-soaked city streets or braving the daily Metro traffic, the VinFast VF 6 is engineered to make the journey more confident, comfortable, and manageable.

articles.title: Lawmakers, lawbreakers
articles.summary: Congress’ power over the budget is supposed to discipline executive spending, not license legislative excess. Yet recent appropriations show how the constitutional ban on increasing the President’s…

blocks.text: Congress’ power over the budget is supposed to discipline executive spending, not license legislative excess. Yet recent appropriations show how the constitutional ban on increasing the President’s proposed budget has been repeatedly blurred, especially through unprogrammed funds and lawmakers’ own institutional budgets.

In a democracy, the power of the purse is meant to be a restraint, not a loophole. Congress authorizes spending so that presidents cannot build roads, erect monuments, or wage wars without public consent. But that power carries a matching duty: to protect taxpayers from waste and to ensure that public money is spent only as the Constitution allows.

The Philippine legislature has wide authority over the budget, taxes, and tariffs. It may decide how large government should be and how much citizens should pay for it, subject to constitutional limits. Its task is not merely to spend, but to make the state deliver value for money.

That discipline begins with the National Expenditure Program (NEP), prepared by the President. The General Appropriations Bill must be based on that proposal. This is not a ceremonial sequence. There can be no budget bill without the President’s submission, and Congress is not free to turn authorization into augmentation.
The rule Congress keeps testing

The constitutional rule is blunt. Article VI, Section 25(1) provides that Congress “may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the Government as specified in the budget.” Yet recent budgets suggest that this rule has been treated less as a command than as an inconvenience.

blocks.caption: Sources: Department of Budget and Management, various budget documents.

blocks.text: Sources: Department of Budget and Management, various budget documents.
A quiet expansion of the budget

In the programmed and automatic portions of the 2023, 2024, and 2025 budgets, Congress broadly kept to the President’s proposal. In 2025 it even approved slightly less than requested: ₱4.222 trillion against ₱4.247 trillion. On its face, that looked compliant.

The real expansion took place in unprogrammed appropriations. Congress added ₱219.0 billion in 2023 (or 37.2 percent), ₱449.5 billion in 2024 (or 159.5 percent), and ₱204.7 billion in 2025 (or 129.0 percent). Over three years, the additions reached ₱873.3 billion—close to ₱1 trillion. The form may have been legislative adjustment; the substance was budget enlargement.
When lawmakers budget for themselves

The Constitution is equally clear on another point: appropriations for Congress must follow the same procedure applied to other departments and agencies. Senators and representatives are not a budgetary class apart. The rules they impose on the Executive should apply, with equal force, to themselves.

Two principles therefore matter: Congress should not increase what the President proposes, and when it budgets for its own institutions, it should undergo the same pre-plenary scrutiny faced by executive departments. Fiscal restraint loses force when its authors exempt themselves from it.

blocks.caption: Legend: SET: Senate Electoral Tribunal; CA: Commission on Appointments; HOR: House of Representatives; HOR ET: House Electoral Tribunal; OP: Office of the President; OVP: Office of the Vice President.

blocks.text: Legend: SET: Senate Electoral Tribunal; CA: Commission on Appointments; HOR: House of Representatives; HOR ET: House Electoral Tribunal; OP: Office of the President; OVP: Office of the Vice President.

The pattern is clearest in the appropriations for the highest offices of government: the President, the Vice President, the Senate, the House, and their related bodies. These figures reveal not merely accounting choices, but the political economy of budgeting.

In the first four national budgets submitted by President Marcos Jr., lawmakers—particularly the Senate, the House, and the Commission on Appointments—approved appropriations above the President’s proposal. The constitutional ceiling became, in practice, a floor.

The fifth budget tells a different story. Lawmakers appear to have observed the “no increase” rule, perhaps chastened by public outrage over the misuse of public funds. That is progress, but not virtue. Obeying the Constitution is the minimum expected of those who write the laws.

The real test is still ahead. Will Congress now allow its own budget to be examined in public before plenary debate, as one legislator has proposed? The Senate and the House have long resisted such scrutiny. If lawmakers want the public to believe they have rediscovered fiscal discipline, they should begin by applying it to themselves.

articles.title: De Lima to DENR: Halt earth-balling of mangroves
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Mamamayang Liberal Rep. Leila de Lima has called for the suspension of “earth-balling” or relocation of mangroves until the Department of Environment and Natural Resources…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Mamamayang Liberal Rep. Leila de Lima has called for the suspension of “earth-balling” or relocation of mangroves until the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) crafts a more comprehensive study on the matter.

At a recent House hearing on the DENR’s proposed 2027 budget, De Lima inquired about the status of the department’s Oct. 8, 2025 memorandum providing guidelines for processing requests to earth-ball mangroves pending the completion of a study.
She wondered why the memorandum was issued despite the lack of scientific studies or even consultations.
De Lima also observed that an “interim operational guidance” has apparently turned into a “de facto policy” allowing the earth-balling of mangroves for flagship infrastructure projects.

“We understand that there is a technical working group (TWG) that was recently created regarding the earth-balling of mangroves. I am wondering why that memorandum was issued at all, even before consultations, or even before the creation of TWG, or a scientific study. What exactly is the survival rate?” she said.
“All of these things should have been confirmed or verified first before allowing the issuance of this memorandum,” she further pointed out.
Commitment to evaluate
In response, Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said the department deemed it appropriate at the time to issue the memorandum in pursuit of sustainable development.

He also claimed the DENR was in consultation with the Ecosystem Research and Development Bureau, Biodiversity Management Bureau and Forest Management Bureau, the agencies tasked to study the survival rate of mangroves.
“We’re encouraged by the initial results that have been sent to us already, but for us to be able to really extensively complete the study, we are targeting December of this year,” he said.
Hearing this, De Lima advised the DENR to be more direct about the study’s findings, especially if the mangroves’ survival rate is extremely low.
She urged the department to “first suspend the implementation, if not do away with the memorandum altogether.”
Cuna committed to evaluate the matter.
House measures

De Lima earlier filed House Resolution No. 1206 seeking to conduct an inquiry into the memorandum as this directly conflicts with the country’s commitments and undermines its standing as a steward of global mangrove conservation.

She also filed House Bill No. 8353 seeking to require the establishment of coastal greenbelt zones to prevent coastal erosion. These zones consist of mangroves and beach forests at least 100 meters wide.
The measure also specifically defines the country’s policy goals and objectives for the management of mangrove resources.

“The lack of a national policy on mangroves poses a great challenge and has caused existing mangrove protection and rehabilitation efforts to remain ineffective and unsuccessful,” De Lima said in filing the bill.
“We must urgently implement a comprehensive mechanism to shield coastal communities, protect habitats, and set the stage for rebuilding our fisheries and achieving food security,” she added.

De Lima had also sought to establish the “legal validity” of the guidelines, citing laws mandating the protection of mangroves such as Republic Act No. 8550, or the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, as amended by RA 10654, and RA 8371, or the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act. /cb

articles.title: QC gov’t to penalize projects that leave behind debris
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Infrastructure projects in Quezon City that leave construction debris, waste or damaged public facilities behind could face penalties and delays in project approval under a new…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Infrastructure projects in Quezon City that leave construction debris, waste or damaged public facilities behind could face penalties and delays in project approval under a new city ordinance.

Quezon City residents and motorists may report such projects that have become obstructions to their convenience and safety via the QCitizen Helpline 122 or by filing a report at quezoncity.gov.ph/program/qc-ireport/.

The city government said all public and private infrastructure projects must secure a Certificate of Site Restoration and Cleanup Compliance (CSRCC) before they can be officially accepted or fully authorized under the Quezon City Construction Site Restoration and Cleanup Compliance Ordinance (SP-3519, S-2026).

The ordinance seeks to prevent construction debris from blocking roads, sidewalks, drainage systems, waterways and other public spaces, which the city government said could worsen flooding and endanger residents.

“Every infrastructure project must be completed in a safe, orderly, and environmentally responsible manner. No developer or project proponent should be allowed to leave behind debris that threatens our people, communities, and environment,” Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said.
Regulations

Under the ordinance, project proponents must clear construction and demolition debris, restore affected roads, sidewalks, drainage systems and rights-of-way, and ensure proper backfilling and compaction.
They must also comply with engineering, environmental and waste management regulations and ensure that debris is transported, disposed of, recovered or recycled only through authorized facilities.

The CSRCC will be issued only after a project secures the required clearances, including a Technical Restoration Clearance from the Quezon City Department of Engineering and an Environmental Compliance Inspection Report from the Department of Sanitation and Cleanup Works of Quezon City.

“The Department of Building Official will oversee privately owned or privately funded projects, while the Quezon City Department of Engineering will have jurisdiction over projects owned or funded by the City Government. District Action Offices and barangays will assist in monitoring and reporting noncompliant projects,” the city government said. /cb

articles.title: Singapore lawyer-diplomat behind Unclos talks wins Magsaysay award
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean lawyer-diplomat Tommy Koh was named one of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardees on Monday for his significant role in guiding the adoption of the United Nations…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Singaporean lawyer-diplomat Tommy Koh was named one of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Awardees on Monday for his significant role in guiding the adoption of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).
The Philippines relies on Unclos as the legal basis for defining its maritime zones, upholding its sovereign rights, and addressing territorial disputes in the West Philippine Sea.
In 1978, Koh chaired a key negotiating committee of the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea and, as its president in 1982, led more than 150 countries in adopting Unclos.

“Of enormous significance to maritime countries, this ‘constitution for oceans’ defined territorial waters and the economic rights of countries to their coastal waters and provides mechanisms for settling disputes,” the Ramon Magsaysay Awards Foundation (RMAF) said in citing Koh’s work.
Koh, a law professor from the National University of Singapore, is also recognized for mentoring a new generation of advocates for justice and human dignity worldwide.
Two other laureates
“Two of Singapore’s founding fathers, Dr. Goh Keng Swee and Mr. Lim San, had won the Award. I feel humbled and happy to join their illustrious company,” said Koh in a statement.
The event on Monday, organized by the RMAF, also recognized Runa Khan from Bangladesh and Bo Kyi from Myanmar as the other two laureates.

Khan, a founder of the grassroots development organization Friendship, was honored for leading Friendship’s work in healthcare, education, climate adaptation, livelihoods, disaster preparedness, and inclusive citizenship among Bangladesh’s poorest communities.

Speaking during a live video call, Khan said she was receiving the award “on behalf of the unaddressed communities, my Friendship family, and all those who have walked beside me on this journey for 25 long years with just faith.”
Kyi, a former political prisoner, was recognized for his lifelong commitment to truth, accountability, and justice through his work on issues related to human rights in Myanmar.

He is also a cofounder of the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an organization that documents political arrests and detentions while providing support to political detainees and their families.
In a statement, Kyi said, “It is a great honor to receive this precious Award, which carries forward the legacy of Ramon Magsaysay, a leader of integrity and courage.”
Kyi was arrested after Myanmar’s 1988 prodemocracy protests and served two prison terms, spending a total of seven years in detention.
November culmination
The 2026 Ramon Magsaysay awardees will receive a medallion featuring President Ramon Magsaysay’s likeness, a citation certificate, and a cash prize.

The 68th Ramon Magsaysay Awards festival season will culminate in November with Festival Week, featuring public lectures by the awardees and ending with the presentation ceremonies on Nov. 15 at the Metropolitan Theater in Manila.

The RMAF honors the legacy of former President Ramon Magsaysay by recognizing individuals and organizations that tackle pressing issues with exceptional dedication, integrity, creativity, and selflessness.

Following the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, the RMAF said the “tragedy is an urgent reminder of the critical need for stronger environment stewardship, climate resilience, and swift humanitarian systems.”

“Today, our hearts are heavy as we stand in deep solidarity with the peoples of Nepal and Tibet, mourning the thousands of lives lost in the recent disaster,” said the RMAF through a video statement. /cb

articles.title: Jacob Elordi's The Dog Stars bombs as audiences redefine what they want
articles.summary: The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend, earning just $19.3M US — a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led…

image.caption: Jacob Elordi stars in Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars. (20th Century Studios/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend, earning just $19.3M US — a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led feature that cost an estimated $80 million US to make. It was one of the most underwhelming openings for a mainstream Hollywood release in a year that hasn't exactly been short of disappointing films.
New post-apocalyptic drama limps through opening weekend in a year that actually saw the movie industry grow
The Dog Stars, 20th Century Fox's post-apocalypse blockbuster blunder, bombed at the box office this weekend with just $19.3M US opening weekend.

It was a dismal start for the Ridley Scott directed, Jacob Elordi-led feature, which Variety estimated cost $80 million US to produce. The movie was one of the most underwhelming openings for a mainstream Hollywood release in 2026 — a year that is in no way short of disappointing films, but that has also seen an unexpected streak of successes.

The movie follows a group of people attempting to survive a post-apocalyptic America after a catastrophic, society-ending pandemic. Its weak showing was forecast shortly before the film debuted. An adaptation of Peter Heller's critically acclaimed novel of the same name, critics roundly pilloried the film for its slow pace, cliche genre stylings and bizarre finale.

The Dog Stars is just the latest in a series of other misses from director Ridley Scott. The Alien creator's last three movies have now been misses at the box office. Napoleon, a retelling of France's infamous emperor; and Gladiator 2, a follow-up to the smash 2000 hit, both commanded surprisingly low numbers.

The Dog Stars' poor turnout put it in league with a number of other flops this year: DC tentpole Supergirl managed a meagre $125 million US off a reported $175 million budget, The Bride earned roughly $24 million US from a $90 million US budget, and Moana drew roughly $309 million US from a $250 million US budget.

items: The only time The Dog Stars isn't boring is when it's bad
The dinosaur sex in The End of Oak Street is odd. The reality is far more confusing

blocks.text: But despite a difficult period for the film industry, those numbers can't be entirely blamed on audiences not showing up. Hits like Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Michael and Toy Story 5 have buoyed 2026 to what may be a banner year; one which numerous outlets have forecast may amount to the best since the start of the pandemic.
When it comes to what's driving that upturn, it generally seems to be following a clear trend.

Unlike recent years, when the domestic box office was dominated almost entirely by sequels and popular franchises like Marvel and Star Wars, the biggest earners in 2026 include a ​larger share of original or standalone films — suggesting audiences are responding to a broader range of theatrical releases.

In general, a stronger and more varied slate of films including low-budget sensations like Backrooms and Obsession, non-franchise successes like Project Hail Mary — and even last week's surprise smash, the anti-capitalist Coyote vs. Acme — have all helped drive box-office ​growth this year.

Domestic box-office revenue in the U.S. reached $6.2 billion US through Aug. 2. That's up 15 per cent from the same period last year, according to media analytics firm Rentrak. In 2019, box office sales topped $7 billion US at the same point in the year.
The English-language Canadian box office akso saw strong gains in 2026, led by narratively unique performers like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, undertone, Little Lorraine and Mile End Kicks.

According to Telefilm Canada's latest Review of Canadian Moviegoing and Distribution, box office gross increased nearly 180 per cent in the first two quarters of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
Coyote vs Acme review: Was it worth the wait?

By the end of December — when Dune 3 and Avengers: Doomsday hit theatres — that could catapult 2026 to a $10 billion US year according to Variety. That box-office increase has not extended to The Dog Stars, even though it's also an offering that's not based on a franchise.

However, its trajectory may point even more clearly toward what audiences are searching for. Most 2026 success stories have either courted controversy for their subject matter, or how they stretched and tested storytelling norms.

The Dog Stars sits closer to other poor performers like Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day or Spielberg-clone The End of Oak Street, which were all criticized for resting their films too centrally on conventional, if nostalgic, storytelling styles.
While harkening back to nostalgia may have been enough to bring in the crowds before, it seems more and more audiences are searching for something new.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: The only Mini 1965 Victory Edition in PH is already sold
articles.summary: Few cars can boast of a racing history quite like the Mini Cooper. Few could have predicted that this little economy car would claim victory in the 1965 Monte Carly Rally and go one to win several…

blocks.text: Drive
PH only gets one of this limited edition Mini Cooper

Few cars can boast of a racing history quite like the Mini Cooper. Few could have predicted that this little economy car would claim victory in the 1965 Monte Carly Rally and go one to win several others from there.

Not surprisingly, Mini is celebrating that historic victory with the unveiling of the Mini 1965 Victory Edition. This limited edition was created to celebrate the legendary Mini Cooper S, driven by Timo Mäkinen and co-driver Paul Easter, that took victory at the 1965 Monte Carlo Rally. It is based on a Mini John Cooper Works edition but features unique details exclusive to the Victory Edition. Powered by 231 hp and 380 Nm of maximum torque, it accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in just 6.1 seconds.

Amont them are Chili Red exterior paintwork, accentuated by a white trim stripe extending from the bonnet to the roof and rear. A white “52” graphic adorns both sides of the vehicle – a reference to the number of the original car displayed from 1965.

The Glazed White roof is offered with a panoramic roof. The subtle “1965” sticker on the C-pillar emphasizes the historic year of victory. The 18-inch alloy wheels give the vehicle a dynamic appearance.

The door sill showcases white “1965” writing on a red and black background. In addition, each model of the edition features a dedication on the inside of the door reflecting information about the momentous rally.

The interior is based on the traditional JCW color palette and the familiar JCW-Trim, finished in anthracite and red. The 6 O´clock spoke of the sports steering wheel and the storage box in the center of the console feature the “1965” lettering. The racing number, 52, of the victorious Mini Cooper S from 1965 adorns the key cap of the exclusive edition.

The Mini 1965 Victory Edition is limited in number, with many countries only getting a handful of units. The Philippines has been given just one. It is priced at P4,649,000. Unfortunately, it is already sold.

Before it heads to its new owner, Mini Philippines is giving fans one last up-close look. A full video walk-through reveal of the Mini 1965 Victory Edition is on the official MINI Philippines Facebook and Instagram pages, as well as the Mini Philippines YouTube channel.

“Winning in Monte Carlo in 1965 wasn’t just a victory, it was also a milestone that shaped MINI’s identity,” said Willy Tee Ten, President of Mini Philippines. “The Mini 1965 Victory Edition brings together the heart and soul of that moment with a modern drive packed with loads of fun. It’s a powerful reminder of the passion that defines Mini and every detail points to the courage and craftsmanship that make the brand truly unique.”
You may be too late for this one, but Mini Philippines promises that three more special edition models are scheduled to be offered locally before the end of the year.

blocks.text: Aid on way to Nepal amid grave concerns for missing Australians, Wong says

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor

An RAAF flight containing hygiene kits, shelter and solar lights will leave for Nepal this morning, as the foreign affairs minister and acting prime minister, Penny Wong, says grave concerns are held over the 43 missing Australians after the Nepal-Tibet flash flood.

More than 4,400 people are still missing on both sides of the border, with more than 930 people confirmed dead. Wong told the ABC’s 7.30 program last night that the federal government is urgently seeking to find the whereabouts of the 43 missing Australians.
She said the Australian government has provided $8m in aid so far and noted that Australian citizens had donated $2m to a public appeal – something that the federal government is matching.
More aid will leave today, she said:

double quotation markWe are deploying an RAAF aircraft to deliver these kits which are designed to support people in circumstances of natural disasters that destroy infrastructure and their shelter. Whether it’s shelter kits, lights, hygiene kits, these are the things needed for those people who are facing the devastation of their homes and their communities.

blocks.caption: Australian aid pallets are loaded at RAAF Base Amberley in response to the catastrophic flooding in Nepal. Photograph: LACW Taylor Anderson

blocks.text: On the 43 missing Australians, Wong said Australia has been engaging with the Nepali and Chinese governments but the recovery and search effort is “very difficult”.
Nine of the 43 missing were on the Chinese side of the border at the time of the floods, but no more information was available on the 43 missing, she said.

double quotation markI first want to again express what I’ve been expressing to the families and friends of the 43 Australians who are not accounted for, that this is such a difficult time, it’s an incredibly distressing, traumatic time. I think all Australians are with you. And certainly we are with you. We are working to do whatever we can and to provide any information we obtain.

blocks.caption: Patrick Commins

blocks.text: Patrick Commins
AI will help boost productivity performance back up to average, Treasury says
Treasury says artificial intelligence will help drag Australia’s productivity performance back to its historical average over coming years, according to departmental briefing papers.
With the government set to release its latest intergenerational report this month, Jim Chalmers said “AI is shaping up to be the biggest economic transformation in our lifetime”.

double quotation markThis is a gamechanging technology which will impact every part of our economy and society, in every corner of our country. I’m confident we can maximise the economic upside and minimise the risks.

blocks.caption: Jim Chalmers. Photograph: AAP

blocks.text: Australia’s productivity growth has stalled, with the nation no more productive now than it was at the beginning of the decade.

Amid a national and sometimes heated debate over the regulation of AI and its related technologies, such as datacentres, the Treasury briefing paper said “AI is the first substantive, credible global productivity growth accelerant in almost two decades”.

But Treasury officials advised that, for now, the adoption of AI across the economy was not expected to usher in a new era of turbocharged growth, even as they flagged the unusually wide range of forecasts.
Instead, the “baseline” forecast was that “AI will support the achievement of the long-term productivity assumption of 1.2%” – a forecast outlined in the lead up to this year’s budget.
NSW workers to march for extra public holiday

The Shop and Warehouse Workers Union (SDA) say over 400 workers will march to NSW parliament on Tuesday with a petition signed by over 10,000 workers and their families to call for an additional public holiday for 1 September.
The union says NSW has the fewest public holidays in any state or territory in Australia, with 11 statewide public holidays, eight of which are in the first half of the year.
The ACT, Victoria, NT and WA have the most at 13.
The union and workers are calling for 1 September to be declared a new public holiday in the state as a “family and community day”.
The petition will be handed to the NSW industrial relations minister, Sophie Cotsis.
SDA NSW/ACT secretary Bernie Smith said:

double quotation markNSW workers work just as hard as everyone else, and they deserve the same opportunities to spend time with their families and friends. Spring is all about new beginnings and that is exactly what a 1 September public holiday would provide for NSW.
Good morning, Nick Visser here to take the blog reins. Let’s giddy up.
Most capital city home prices fall below $1m in August

blocks.caption: Luca Ittimani

blocks.text: Luca Ittimani
The typical capital city home price has slipped back below $1m as buyers fail to show up in a “buyers’ market”, property data firm Cotality has reported.

The median price in the capitals surpassed $1m for the first time back in October but has steadily fallen this year with demand suppressed by rising interest rates and weak confidence in the economy. By the end of August, it fell to $990,394, Cotality found.
The typical home price in Perth passed $1m in March, but slipped to $999,987 by the end of August.

Sydney and Brisbane are back to being the only capitals with median prices above $1m. Sydney’s is at $1.22m, $93,000 below its peak earlier this year, while Brisbane is at $1.08m, down $30,000 from its peak.

Cotality’s research director, Tim Lawless, said nearly every capital city suburb had now seen prices fall, yet far fewer homes were being sold compared with this time last year, meaning listings on the market were building up. He said:

double quotation markLonger selling times, larger vendor discounting and persistently low auction clearance rates all point to a buyer’s market, yet buyers are lacking the confidence to transact at the moment.

blocks.caption: Adeshola Ore

blocks.text: Adeshola Ore
Nepali and Tibetan communities mourn in Melbourne
Members of Melbourne’s Nepali and Tibetan communities gathered in the city’s Federation Square last night to remember the victims of the Nepal-Tibet flood.
More than 40 Australians are among thousands of people who remain missing after the natural disaster last week. The overall death toll is at least 810 people.
At the vigil, volunteers unfurled a sign on the ground – encircled by candlelight – that read “Vic united for Nepal”.
The event, organised by the Non-Resident Nepali Association’s Victorian branch, was attended by the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, and Labor and opposition MPs.
Speaking to the crowd of about 400 people, Carroll said:

double quotation markI know so many of your hearts are breaking right now. Look around you, all of Victoria stands behind you and every candle in Federation Square is lit up for you. You are not alone.
Carroll said the Victoria government had pledged to donate $100,000 to Australia’s immediate efforts in Nepal.

blocks.caption: The crowd raises their phone lights and candles at a candlelight vigil in Melbourne for victims of the Nepal floods on Monday evening. Photograph: Josh Stanyer/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: ‘A lot of anger … but very few real solutions’, Wong says of Hanson
Penny Wong has said Labor accepts there’s a message from WA Labor’s loss to One Nation in the Secret Harbour byelection, but says the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has “very few real solutions”.
Wong told ABC’s 7.30 program the loss was “very disappointing”, but that Labor knows many Australians “believe the status quo is not delivering for them”.

blocks.caption: Foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong. Photograph: Michael Errey/AAP

blocks.text: She pointed to policies such a investment in Medicare, childcare and schools, as well as tax cuts and tax changes as the federal government’s response. Wong accepted that the public had not taken the changes on board in their vote in WA, but said Hanson was not offering solutions.
She said:

double quotation markI accept there’s a message sent in this byelection for us. I accept that. And I think we understand that. We understand the importance of delivering real change and as someone who sits in the Senate with Pauline Hanson, what I would say to you is that she is … there’s a lot of anger and a lot of complaints, but really very few solutions.
