articles.title: The Canadian suspected of spying on NATO was denied bail. Here’s what comes next
articles.byline: Aloysius Wong, Albert Leung, Idil Mussa

image.caption: 33-year-old computer scientist Biwei Zhang lost an appeal for release from pretrial detention in Belgium amid allegations of spying on NATO's military headquarters, where she was working as an intern. (Reuters, Catina Zhang/Facebook)

blocks.text: The Canadian suspected of spying on the NATO military headquarters in Belgium is expected to remain in detention until her trial, which could be a year or more away.
Biwei Zhang, 33, will remain in custody after a Belgian judge on Monday denied the former NATO intern’s appeal for release.
"Today, the Chamber of Indictments decided to extend the suspect’s pretrial detention by one month," the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Zhang must appear before a judge at regular intervals — once a month for the first three months and every two months thereafter — to determine whether pretrial detention remains appropriate.
Because of the seriousness of the allegations and the risk that the suspect may abscond, it is "rather unlikely" that Zhang will be released before the trial, one Belgian legal expert told CBC News.

"If they have a serious case with lots of indications that she might have committed an offence, then it will be hard to be released before the trial," said Frank Verbruggen, a criminal law professor at KU Leuven, a Catholic research university in Leuven, Belgium.
The trial likely won’t begin until sometime next year "at the earliest," he said.
Unlike in Canada, Belgian courts do not name criminal defendants until trial.

However, CBC News was first to identify the suspect as Biwei Zhang — also known by the names Claire and Catina — an intern at NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) with a background in computer science and economics.

The Canadian woman was arrested on July 24, a day after her home and workplace were searched, and was subsequently charged by Belgian authorities with "spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization."
CBC News identifies Canadian intern accused of spying on NATO
Sources have told Reuters and other media that the suspected third country is China.
The Chinese embassy in Canada told CBC it firmly opposes the "baseless speculations and smears against China."
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Neither Zhang nor her lawyer responded to CBC News requests for comment.
Espionage 'test case'

Verbruggen says the criminal organization charge is one Belgian prosecutors charge "very often," as it is defined broadly as an association of more than two people working together to commit certain offences.
"That has the advantage that the number of investigative methods, for instance, like infiltration or covert observation and so on, are quite easy to justify," he said.

But Verbruggen says the spying charges against Zhang will likely be a "test case" for Belgian courts, as definitions of espionage were updated in 2024 to account for modern techniques of intelligence gathering.
Why prosecuting spy cases makes it harder to keep information secret
He says espionage cases are "very rare," as criminal prosecution of spies is often considered a last resort, with authorities more likely to remove or monitor them instead.
"There is a kind of understanding that it's better to know who's spying on you and tolerate them and keep an eye on them than to expel them and then get new ones."
The case has also raised questions about the efficacy of Canada’s security screening, which was responsible for clearing Zhang for her NATO position.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this month that although he is limited in what he can disclose amid the active investigation, "Canadian officials have been involved from the start."
Canada involved 'from the start' in investigation of NATO intern accused of spying: Carney

The House of Commons standing committee on public safety and national security is set to convene to review Canada’s screening processes after opposition parties called for an emergency meeting following the spying allegations.

Former CSIS intelligence officer Dan Stanton, who has no direct knowledge of the case, speculates it’s possible Zhang was identified "quite some time ago" and that "there could be a very complicated counterintelligence operation in the background."

items: Ottawa will look into screening processes amid NATO intern spying allegations
Conservatives, Bloc want probe into Canadian NATO intern spying allegations

blocks.text: Suspect may have 'crossed the line' later
Prior to moving to Europe, Zhang worked as a public servant at multiple federal government agencies in Canada.

This included data scientist jobs at both Employment and Social Development Canada and Statistics Canada, and later work as a systems engineer for the Canadian Space Agency, according to her LinkedIn profile as well as her CV, which was included in a federal court case.

None of the three agencies would confirm details about the suspect but told CBC they will continue to collaborate with domestic and international partners "to protect national security and preserve the integrity of the investigative process."

Stanton, now the director of the national security program at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute, said if Zhang was indeed spying for a foreign power, another possibility is that she was recruited more recently.
"They may have, on paper in terms of initial vetting, been fine, but at some point maybe they were cultivated and recruited by a hostile intelligence service."

The federal court documents also included a report from the Public Service Commission of Canada, which concluded that Zhang had committed fraud by applying for the same government job under two names and emails.

items: CBC identifies Canadian woman accused of spying at NATO military HQ
Canadian intern at NATO military headquarters in Belgium faces spying charges

blocks.text: In an apology letter to an investigator included in court filings, Zhang described herself as a young professional "passionate about using the power of data to drive public policy with an ambitious, innovative mind."
Stanton says it's "quite possible" this is a case where a Canadian decided to spy after having a negative experience working for the government.
"There may be some revenge-seeking here with this individual, and then they crossed the line and became an insider threat," he said.
NATO spy suspect possibly recruited after she was vetted, says ex-CSIS officer
Zhang had been working in SHAPE’s IT department, according to Reuters.

European media have reported that Zhang allegedly exhibited suspicious behaviour that triggered the investigation, such as asking questions about SHAPE’s security and entering off-limits areas. After her apartment was searched, Zhang’s home was reportedly broken into by suspected accomplices.

It is unclear whether Zhang will be prosecuted under Belgium’s old criminal code or its new one, which goes into force in September. Each code contains several spying offences with different maximum penalties.

Depending on whether there are any alleged aggravating factors, Verbruggen expects Zhang could face up to a decade in prison if convicted of espionage or three years' imprisonment for working with a criminal organization.
Given the sensitivity of what the suspect might have accessed, Verbruggen says prosecutors may want to avoid a public trial or pivot to other offences like hacking to keep more information secret.
"Many people are involved in a criminal trial. The fear of leaks or the risk that information is leaked is always there."

articles.title: Triple whammy
articles.summary: #MINDANAO While millions are reeling from the effects of flooding traumas in Central Luzon and Metro Manila, we have higher interest rates and the record low of the Philippine peso against the US…

blocks.text: #MINDANAO

While millions are reeling from the effects of flooding traumas in Central Luzon and Metro Manila, we have higher interest rates and the record low of the Philippine peso against the US Dollar. This makes these an unwelcome triple whammy. I will try to help us understand what this will mean for many of us who are consumers.
The first whammy: A devalued peso and our oil prices

I know that as an oil importing country needing to pay already high prices for imported oil, a peso devaluation is an unwanted development since it forces us to pay more for the already expensive barrel of oil we import.

This can translate to higher prices of gasoline and diesel fuel, and perhaps increased prices of public transport and the cost of transporting food commodities such as rice, eggs and vegetables all a potential dagger at the heart of consumers. Entrepreneurs will need to prepare for higher prices of inputs and other costs. Workers may demand even higher wages.
A weaker peso may also increase the import costs of other commodities as businesses will need to pay more pesos for thensame metric ton of whatever commodity is imported.

As a result, there may be pressure to increase the prices of products and services being provided. The cascade of higher prices will hurt the majority the consumers. Thus, how these increases may take place and the pains they bring will play out in the coming weeks bears our thoughtful attention.

Curiously though, currencies of our neighbors such as Malaysia have appreciated against the dollar, giving them the extra buffer against higher import prices. How and why our currency fell and theirs rose will need to be answered. Read on this here:https://mb.com.ph/2026/08/31/philippine-peso-asias-worst-performing-currencyjapanese-bank
The second whammy: Higher interest rates

The second whammy comes for businesses as interest rates have been pushed up to five percent by the bangko sentral, a move supposedly aimed at taming inflation. Please read the MB article on this for further reference. (https://mb.com.ph/2026/08/27/bsp-raises-interest-rate-to-5-to-tame-price-risks)

How this matters to us as consumers is how this increases borrowing costs especially for MSMEs that depend on commercial loans to fund working capital requirements. This is the money to buy the materials needed to make the products, provide services, patñy staff salaries and deliver to customers.
The third whammy: Floods in our three largest regional economies

Both of these whammies come at a time when our largest and most affluent regional economies, namely CALBARZON, Central Luzon and the National Capital Region have been devastated by persistent floods owing to the monsoons over a two week period. These economies are where we have the bigfest volumes of spending, somethi g we need to do to generate incomes and growth. Suppressed spending by people may lead to stagnation and reduced incomes for others.

Whether this is the knife edge of the dreaded super El Nino weather phenomenon is debatable, but recovering from the effects on these economies will take time and potentially shave off badly needed growth, as it comes at a time when we need to catch up on anemic growth.
Moving forward
As we enter the ber months, there is a hope that the effects of these whammies will abate and that we can recover, and hopefully adapt to the new realities shaping up from these events.

articles.title: AICON 2026: Building the AI Ready Philippines
articles.summary: TECH4GOOD The recently concluded AICON 2026 was a defining moment for the Philippine technology community. With over 1,000 delegates in attendance, the event was certainly one of the largest…

blocks.text: TECH4GOOD

The recently concluded AICON 2026 was a defining moment for the Philippine technology community. With over 1,000 delegates in attendance, the event was certainly one of the largest AI-related conferences we have had in the country so far, a clear indication that Filipinos are not just curious about artificial intelligence but are determined to learn how to shape it, live it, and use it responsibly.

Organized by the Analytics and AI Association of the Philippines, which today has more than 2,000 individual and corporate members, this year’s flagship event centered on the theme: “Human by Design: Building the AI Future We Choose.” The unexpectedly large attendance signaled an unmistakable shift in public mindset. The hunger to learn about artificial intelligence is no longer confined to specialized tech circles. For most, AI is no longer a distant concept but a present reality demanding thoughtful action.

The event also drew strong support from key players in the Philippine AI ecosystem: leading enterprises, technology providers, and institutions investing in the country’s AI capabilities. Their demonstration booths gave delegates the opportunity to experience these capabilities firsthand.

AICON 2026 showcased diverse strategies for implementing AI in enterprises. A primary focus throughout the conference was translating technological promise into measurable outcomes for enterprises. Business leaders engaged in candid discussions and shared strategies for embedding AI into organizational workflows to maximize performance and value.

Some conversations focused on incremental automation, embedding AI into existing workflows to optimize efficiency. Others pursued enterprise agentification, scaling AI agents across departments to handle specific tasks while ensuring humans remain in charge of direction and accountability. This balance between autonomy and oversight was a recurring theme. Yes, it automates routine tasks yet demands new forms of human oversight. It augments creativity but forces us to ask: what remains uniquely ours? The conversations emphasized that the human dimension remains central. AI can execute, but humans must govern. As one speaker put it, “AI can take charge of work, but only humans can remain in charge.”

A session explored how making AI a practical teammate requires a shift in leadership mindsets. Rather than treating tools as mere software utilities, companies are coaching employees to collaborate with AI agents as adaptive co-workers—optimizing speed and accuracy while safeguarding human oversight.

The conference devoted significant attention to talent sustainability and nation-building initiatives. The urgency of workforce development dominated discussions. The Philippines, with its globally competitive BPO sector, stands at a crossroads. Will AI displace jobs—or elevate them? Leaders argued for the latter. By retraining workers to supervise, fine-tune, and collaborate with AI systems, the country can build an AI-ready workforce. The presentation on how the Philippine Qualifications Framework complements the Philippine Skills Framework was much appreciated for detailing pathways that bridge formal education and practical industry skill sets.

A homegrown BPO operator demonstrated how local outsourcing companies are using AI to scale human talent rather than reduce headcount. By automating routine tasks, Filipino BPO professionals can move up the value chain into higher-tier advisory, technical, and analytical roles. Experts also mapped out emerging roles that blend technical proficiency with domain expertise, emphasizing that adaptability and digital literacy are vital for future career security.

AICON 2026 did not shy away from hard questions. Panels on AI safety and governance emphasized the need for clear accountability frameworks, bias audits, and transparent decision-making. Becoming an ethical AI professional was presented as a new career imperative: practitioners must recognize that algorithms inherit the biases, blind spots, and values of their creators. Guardrails must be built into the system architecture from day one. In an era of rapid automation, trust is the ultimate competitive advantage.

AICON 2026 also stood out for its commitment to local impact and practical execution. Sessions featured insights from Philippine AI use cases, demonstrating how local institutions across banking, telecommunications, agriculture, and retail are applying data models to solve local challenges.

AICON 2026 delivered a clear message: the future of AI in the Philippines is not a predetermined path dictated by outside tech hubs but a deliberate choice shaped by local decisions. It matters because it catalyzed that choice. By convening government, industry, academia, and civil society, it became a platform for creating a shared vision for an AI-ready Philippines. It reminded us that innovation is not inevitable—it is intentional. The unexpectedly large attendance proved the hunger for knowledge and the urgency of action.

Ultimately, the event lived up to its theme: "Human by Design: Building the AI Future We Choose". By focusing on human-centered progress, AICON 2026 charted a clear path forward—ensuring that as the Philippines advances into an AI-driven era, its technology elevates, empowers, and enriches every Filipino worker and enterprise.
The author is an executive member of the National Innovation Council and lead convener of the Alliance for Technology Innovators for the Nation (ATIN). [email protected]

articles.title: Latest science on Dengvaxia
articles.summary: UNDER THE MICROSCOPE The Dengvaxia controversy continues to simmer, thanks to new cases filed in court and the Sandigabayan recently, and the pronouncements of a self-proclaimed “vaccine expert” who…

blocks.text: UNDER THE MICROSCOPE

The Dengvaxia controversy continues to simmer, thanks to new cases filed in court and the Sandigabayan recently, and the pronouncements of a self-proclaimed “vaccine expert” who still claims Dengvaxia caused deaths among those vaccinated.

But there have been no valid scientific studies published in reputable medical journals to validate these claims of excess deaths due to possible “worsening of dengue signs and symptoms” due to dengue-naïve persons (persons with no prior dengue infection) being vaccinated with Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV), as Dengvaxia manufacturer Sanofi has announced in its supplemental warning in November 2017.

However, the latest valid scientific study on this subject published in the journal Vaccine, volume 56, May 2025 titled “Effectiveness of a single-dose dengue vaccination in Cebu, Philippines: Final results of a five-year case control study” gives us the perspective of what has happened in the five years since the Dengvaxia vaccination program was suspended.

This study involves a rigorous case control study that pairs a group of 584 who were given only one dose of Dengvaxia with 1168 control subjects (not given Dengvaxia). Both groups had virologically confirmed dengue (VCD). The VCD subjects presented as dengue with earning signs (DWS) (eight cases or 1.4 percent), severe dengue eight (1.4 percent) and death due to dengue (1 case or 0.2 percent).

This scientific research was done after the suspension of the Dengvaxia vaccination program that left the Cebu subjects with only the first dose of Dengvaxia and aims to determine the five-year effectiveness of a single dose of CYD-TDV against hospitalized VCD.

The authors who are from the University of the Philippines National Institutes of Health, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champagne, Research Institute of Tropical Medicine, Cebu Provincial Hospital and Eversley Childs Sanitorium and General Hospital, Mandaue City, had previously reported interim (first year) vaccine effectiveness against hospitalized VCD and dengue with warning signs in 2020 was 26 percent and 51 percent respectively in this journal. This recently published study followed through on that study to determine if one dose of Dengvaxia continued to be effective five years after vaccination because data on the long-term effectiveness of incomplete vaccination in the real-world setting was limited.

These effectivity rates were lower than those given the complete three doses which protected against hospitalized VCD and dengue with warning signs at 80 percent. But this is perfectly understandable due to only a single dose administered versus the recommended three doses. The subjects’ immune systems were only primed by the first dose but could not ramp up immunity due to lack of additional stimulation by second and third doses. This is basic immunology.

In this new study, overall vaccine effectiveness against hospitalization was 21 percent in those given one dose of Dengvaxia even after five years. It must be stated that immunity wanes naturally post-vaccination but will increase immune responses if re-stimulated by another dose of vaccine or a re-infection. This is borne out by the higher protection in the first-year post-vaccination at 49 percent. The new data attests to durability of partial protection in the context of the incomplete vaccination schedule.
As of this date, there has been no published data on whether there have been deaths causally attributed to dengue and not just a temporal relationship but with different cause of death.

The main problem was the lack of context in the issuance of an update information on Dengvaxia by Sanofi Inc. It cited the possibility of severe dengue in those vaccinated but had no detailed explanation whether it was supported by clinical trial data.

This study did not see any increased incidence in severe dengue nor any increase in complications or deaths. In fact, it showed a significantly lower proportion of the presence of warning signs and less severe illness among those who received at least one dose of the vaccine.

So, here we are with a valid scientific study done under the most rigorous conditions showing that even one dose of Dengvaxia conferred some degree of immunity and did not show any increased incidence of severe dengue nor any increase in complications or deaths.
Yet, the witch hunt continues targeting even researchers who didn’t have anything to do with procurement and who were just doing basic research on vaccine effectiveness.

People can’t seem to distinguish between good science and the shrill pronouncements of people intent on besmirching good people’s reputations to endear themselves to authorities who they want to influence to appoint them to juicy government positions.

It is time to uphold the validity of science and not believe just anyone who wants to create panic and confusion that led to widespread vaccine hesitancy. The latter has now led to lower vaccination rates against common childhood diseases, resulting in several measles outbreaks which killed several thousand children during the years following the 2017 brouhaha over Dengvaxia.
Please believe the science, not the witchcraft.
Science saves lives. Misinformation kills.

articles.title: He spoke with authority
articles.summary: REFLECTIONS TODAY It is the Season of Creation again! Two years ago, the Church celebrated the Season of Creation with the theme “To Hope and Act with Creation.” Hope is the very impulse that compels…

blocks.text: REFLECTIONS TODAY

It is the Season of Creation again! Two years ago, the Church celebrated the Season of Creation with the theme “To Hope and Act with Creation.” Hope is the very impulse that compels us to do something that the darkness of despair which characterizes our world today might be dispelled. Pope Francis points out in Laudate Deum that while our world is already collapsing, our Christian responses to the present climate crisis remain to be inadequate (n. 2). We can only heed the call to ecological conversion upon recognizing the authority of Jesus’ word, enabling us to act while keeping our hope alive. Hope translated into action is liberating.

In today’s Gospel, the authority of Jesus’ word is demonstrated when he cures a demoniac. “Be quiet!” (v 35), Jesus commands the demon. The Greek verb used is phimoõ, “to muzzle.” Jesus’ command to be silent is restrictive. Whenever we recognize the authority of Jesus’ word, our selfish inclinations are restrained.
Do we want to have a healthier relationship with the environment? Are we ready to submit ourselves to the authority of Jesus’ word? Are we willing to have our consumeristic inclination be restrained?
First Reading • 1 Cor 2:10b-16

Brothers and sisters: 10The Spirit scrutinizes everything, even the depths of God. Among men, who knows what pertains to the man except his spirit that is within? Similarly, no one knows what pertains to God except the Spirit of God. We have not received the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may understand the things freely given us by God. And we speak about them not with words taught by human wisdom, but with words taught by the Spirit, describing spiritual realities in spiritual terms.

Now the natural man does not accept what pertains to the Spirit of God, for to him it is foolishness, and he cannot understand it, because it is judged spiritually. The one who is spiritual, however, can judge everything but is not subject to judgment by anyone.
For “who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to counsel him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
Responsorial Psalm • Ps 145
“The Lord is just in all his ways.”
Gospel • Lk 4:31-37

Jesus went down to Capernaum, a town of Galilee. He taught them on the sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching because he spoke with authority. In the synagogue there was a man with the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out in a loud voice, “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebuked him and said, “Be quiet! Come out of him!” Then the demon threw the man down in front of them and came out of him without doing him any harm. They were all amazed and said to one another, “What is there about his word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out.” And news of him spread everywhere in the surrounding region.
Source: “365 Days with the Lord 2026,” St. Paul’s, 7708 St. Paul Rd., SAV, Makati City (Phils.); Tel.: 632-895-9701; E-mail: [email protected]; Website: http://www.stpauls.ph.

articles.title: ‘Maluwalhating Pilipinas’
articles.summary: FINDING ANSWERS During yesterday’s observance of National Heroes Day, my thoughts were on the many great Filipinos like Dr. Jose Rizal, Andres Bonifacio, and Gabriela Silang whose courage and…
articles.byline: Former Senator Atty. Joey D. Lina

blocks.text: FINDING ANSWERS

During yesterday’s observance of National Heroes Day, my thoughts were on the many great Filipinos like Dr. Jose Rizal, Andres Bonifacio, and Gabriela Silang whose courage and sacrifices helped shape our nation.

Looking back at their heroism—how they gave their wisdom, strength, and lives for their unwavering love for the country—inspired me to create a song in their honor called Maluwalhating Pilipinas (Glorious Philippines).

Co-written with my nephew Robert David, who also composed the music, the song, now available on YouTube, is dedicated to every Filipino who continues to believe in and love our country amid all its difficulties and setbacks.
It is a song that should also make us ask what we are doing with the country our heroes entrusted to us—and what kind of Philippines we will leave to those who come after us.

“Hindi pa huli ang lahat, / Kayang-kaya nating umangat. / Habang may pag-ibig sa bayan, / Ating pag-asa ay tiyak magliliwanag.” (“It’s not too late, / We can rise above it all. / As long as there is love for the nation, / Our hope will surely shine.”) These are the opening lines of the song.
Yes, an overwhelming love of country gives Filipinos great hope that enormous challenges, no matter how seemingly insurmountable, can be overcome.

“Halina, kabayan, tayo’y magsimula, / Ibangon ang dangal ng ating bansa. / Sa tulong ng Diyos at pananampalataya, / Muling wawagayway ang ating bandila.” (“Come, countrymen, let us begin, / Raise the honor of our nation. / With the help of God and faith, / Our flag will wave again.”) These words reverberate in the succeeding verse.

Indeed, the song calls on all Filipinos to act on what keeps the country from moving forward, not surrender to the darkness, disorder, and wrongdoing around us, and instead summon faith in God, renewal, and the determination to rise again.

The ideal love of country is not simply loving the Philippines when things are going well. It is loving the country enough to help correct what is wrong with it. It is choosing honesty when dishonesty is easier, service when selfishness is more rewarding, and hope when cynicism is more fashionable.
Maluwalhating Pilipinas is a call to responsibility. And that responsibility falls heavily on the generation that will inherit the country.

Filipinos of every age can be heroes, but young people possess a special potential. They have the energy, idealism, and courage to imagine a better Philippines—and the time to help make that vision real.

Jose Rizal understood this. In El Filibusterismo, through the character of Padre Florentino, he asked where the young were who would devote their golden years, enthusiasm, and dreams to the welfare of their native land.
More than a century later, we should be asking the same question. Where are the young Filipinos who will devote their talents not only to personal success but also to nation-building?

The Constitution recognizes their importance. Article II, Section 13, declares that the State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and shall encourage their participation in public and civic affairs while inculcating patriotism and nationalism.

The youth today also possess tools that previous generations could scarcely imagine. Social media and information technology can reach millions in an instant. They can educate, expose wrongdoing, and mobilize people around worthy causes. But these same tools can also spread falsehood, deepen divisions, and turn public discourse into an endless contest of outrage.

The choice belongs to the young. They can use technology merely to consume, or they can use it to create. They can amplify noise, or amplify truth. They can remain spectators, or become active participants in shaping the nation.

Our history shows what young Filipinos can accomplish when they choose to participate actively. Rizal, Bonifacio, Emilio Jacinto, Apolinario Mabini, and Gregorio del Pilar were young when they contributed greatly to the struggle against Spanish colonial rule.

Macario Sakay and Miguel Malvar continued the resistance during the American occupation. Countless young Filipinos fought during World War II. Later generations, including the youth of the 1970s and 1980s, my generation, also stood against oppression.
Each generation faced different circumstances, but the responsibility is essentially the same: to help build a country worthy of the sacrifices of those who came before.
Let us all do our part to fulfill the dream handed down to us: a country that is more prosperous, more just, more honorable—truly a “Maluwalhating Pilipinas.” ([email protected])

articles.title: Safeguarding public money demands more than promises
articles.summary: The start of deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget comes at a particularly sensitive moment. There is something profoundly ironic in the spectacle of Cabinet secretaries…

blocks.text: The start of deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget comes at a particularly sensitive moment. There is something profoundly ironic in the spectacle of Cabinet secretaries having to assure Congress that they will conduct lifestyle checks, enforce a one-strike policy and protect public funds from abuse.

Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon has told lawmakers that the agency is continuously conducting lifestyle checks, in coordination with the Office of the Ombudsman, and has adopted a one-strike policy against verified wrongdoing. He has also declared that the proposed 2027 DPWH budget contains no “leadership fund” and no allocations based on the controversial parametric formula.

Should this not be a given? Public officials do not need to be reminded that government money belongs to the people. They do not need extraordinary instructions to exercise integrity. And taxpayers should not have to depend on the personal assurances of Cabinet secretaries that billions in appropriations will not become instruments for corruption, political patronage or private enrichment.
Yet this is where we find ourselves.

Commitments to allocate and disburse public funds judiciously are welcome. But they should be regarded as the minimum, not the achievement. The bigger question is: Why did the system ever permit arrangements that made such assurances necessary?
The answer must involve not only the Executive branch but Congress itself.

The national budget is where government priorities become actual expenditures. It is also where political influence can be converted into projects, allocations and contracts. The revelations and allegations surrounding the previous DPWH budgets have exposed how vulnerable this process can become when institutional safeguards are weakened or circumvented.

Congress therefore cannot simply demand assurances from Cabinet secretaries and then proceed with business as usual. Every proposed project must have a demonstrable public purpose, technical justification, proper costing and transparent implementation.
Most important, Congress must be prepared to subject itself to the same transparency standards it demands from the Executive.

There should be no privileged category of public money. If a government employee must justify an unexplained increase in wealth, why should a politically connected contractor, intermediary or beneficiary be treated differently? If a DPWH official faces dismissal for a verified offense, why should political influence provide a shield to anyone who participates in manipulating public expenditures?
A genuine one-strike policy should apply to corruption wherever it is found; it must be enforced without fear or favor.

They should be supported by systematic examination of Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, procurement records, beneficial ownership, project costs and actual project accomplishments. Technology should make it possible to connect the money trail from appropriation to implementation.

Where wrongdoing is established, accountability must not end with administrative sanctions. Public funds must be recovered. Cases must be prosecuted. Those responsible must face the consequences prescribed by law.

Congress must also be reminded that the people are not merely watching how the Executive and the government bureaucracy spends their money. They are also demanding accountability from their representatives and senators in judiciously allocating public funds.

The 2027 budget must, therefore, become a test of institutional integrity. It is a litmus test on how the citizenry regards their government’s capacity to render genuine public service that addresses basic needs adequately. It demands transparency, accountability and performance.

articles.title: The issue of systems losses, part 1
articles.summary: One of the most applauded announcements of President Marcos Jr. in his penultimate State of the Nation Address (SONA) was his call urging Congress to immediately amend the Electric Power Industry…

blocks.text: One of the most applauded announcements of President Marcos Jr. in his penultimate State of the Nation Address (SONA) was his call urging Congress to immediately amend the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) to stop distribution utilities from passing on system losses and the corresponding value-added tax (VAT) to consumers. The rationale given by the President is straightforward: “it is not the consumer’s fault that a system loss occurred,” and households should not pay for electricity that never reaches them.

However, the proposed solution is not as simple as it sounds. Private distribution companies—represented by Meralco Chairman Manuel V. Pangilinan—immediately responded by highlighting a fundamental technical reality: “When you push electricity through copper wires, there will be resistance. The longer the lines are, the more losses there will be. It is not a question of inefficiency; it is just the way it is, and there’s a cost to it. So the real question is: who bears the cost?” One could just as validly argue that “it is not the distributor’s fault that a technical system loss occurred.”

System loss is the difference between the electricity entering a distribution network (whether belonging to a private utility or an electric cooperative) and the volume billed to customers. It stems from two sources: technical losses caused by line resistance, transformers, and aging equipment; and non-technical losses resulting from electricity theft, illegal connections, defective meters, and billing errors. Meralco’s system loss charges account for about five percent of monthly bills—well below the 6.5 percent cap set by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC). By contrast, some provincial electric cooperatives register system losses as high as 16 percent.

Fortunately for non-specialists in energy economics, two of the field's most knowledgeable professionals—Dr. Ricardo Barcelona and Atty. Monalisa Dimalanta—offered valuable clarity in a recent paper titled “Systems Losses and Market Discipline: Reforming Loss Recovery, Utility Accountability, and Philippine Power-Market Design.” Dr. Barcelona is a banker and business school professor specializing in energy economics, while Atty. Dimalanta is a former Chairperson and CEO of the ERC.

They remind us that system losses are not merely a billing dispute; they are a test of whether regulation enforces discipline on inefficient operators or allows the costs of weak governance, theft, and operational neglect to be passed on to consumers. They propose a core policy standard: consumers should only pay for efficient, benchmarked technical losses, whereas avoidable commercial losses should be absorbed by power suppliers, operators, shareholders, and lenders. This comprehensive framework connects system-loss regulation, market discipline, regulatory reform, grid investment, and cooperative restructuring into a single legislative rationale.

To grasp this issue, laypeople must understand how competitive power markets operate. The current market structure in the Philippine energy sector stems from the thoroughgoing deregulation, liberalization, and privatization enacted during the administration of the late President Fidel V. Ramos—arguably the most effective post-war administration from an economic development standpoint.

Under the competitive market design established by EPIRA, generation prices are set by the marginal supplier in each trading period, and dispatch follows an economic merit order: lower-cost, highly efficient generators supply power first, while higher-cost plants operate only when demand spikes. The mechanics are straightforward: efficiency is rewarded, and inefficiency is exposed. Low-cost generators earn higher dispatch volumes and stronger revenues, while structurally uncompetitive suppliers face lower utilization, squeezed margins, and eventual insolvency if underperformance persists.

The same logic applies to system losses. Power supply pricing covers fixed-cost recovery, variable operating costs, fuel (where applicable), and the efficient technical losses inherent to operating a network. The fundamental policy question is not whether losses exist, but whether the permitted recovery levels are efficient, transparent, and appropriately allocated. Once framed this way, system losses cease to be an emotional billing controversy and become a standard test of regulatory architecture.

Reducing system losses to zero is physically impossible because electricity delivery relies on an integrated production and supply chain. Power plants must generate more energy than end-users consume because plant operations, auxiliary services, network equipment, and physical delivery constraints use up power long before it hits household meters. Once losses breach efficient thresholds, the issue shifts from engineering constraints to regulatory accountability.

Among power plants (whether fueled by coal, diesel, solar, or other renewables), technical losses are typically modest and limited to plant operation and auxiliary services. In contrast, transmission and distribution losses are far higher due to the physical complexity of grid delivery. While efficient urban distribution systems operate at low loss levels, weak grids or poorly maintained systems cannot—as seen in several struggling electric cooperatives. Efficient technical losses represent a legitimate cost of reliable energy supply; conversely, commercial losses driven by theft, poor collections, or governance failures represent management breakdowns and should never qualify for automatic cost recovery.

This principle applies most directly to transmission and distribution networks—the “wires” businesses (such as Meralco) that operate as natural monopolies. Because captive customers cannot choose an alternative distributor, regulators must simulate market discipline through rate formulas that reward efficiency and punish underperformance.

One standard tool is the RPI-X formula used across liberalized power markets. Its logic is simple: a reference price is established for a regulatory period, adjusted annually for inflation, and reduced by an efficiency factor (X) that reflects expected productivity gains. For instance, a ₱10/kWh reference price, combined with six percent inflation and a two percent efficiency factor, yields a Year 1 price of ₱10.4/kWh. This predictable model gives utilities clear parameters to plan capital investments while incentivizing them to beat efficiency targets and retain the financial upside.

Under this setup, system loss management becomes a test of corporate governance rather than an automatic pass-through entitlement. If a utility drives losses below the benchmark, it keeps the savings; if it underperforms, shareholders absorb the loss instead of shifting the burden to rate-payers.

This model explains why networks with high initial loss rates can handle higher efficiency targets: during early liberalization phases, substantial efficiency gains are achievable. Targeted capital expenditure, modern metering, aggressive theft reduction, and professionalized management can cut losses faster than inflation drives up operational costs—a vital mechanism during periods of high inflation driven by external geopolitical or climate shocks.

Unfortunately, current Philippine regulatory practice undermines this incentive framework whenever tariff recovery functions as a guaranteed cost-plus safety net. When excess, preventable losses are routinely passed on to consumers, a distributor's operational shortcomings become the public's financial burden. Conversely, when loss recovery is strictly capped and benchmarked, management gains a direct financial incentive to invest, enforce, collect, and minimize losses.
(To be continued)

articles.title: Building through uncertainty and restoring stability
articles.summary: The Philippine housing industry remains under pressure as millions of families struggle to find decent and affordable homes. With the housing backlog still stuck at 6.5 million units based on United…

blocks.text: The Philippine housing industry remains under pressure as millions of families struggle to find decent and affordable homes. With the housing backlog still stuck at 6.5 million units based on United Nations estimates, government and private developers are increasing home production as demand continues to outpace supply. But the challenge now is to build houses that Filipinos can afford, live in, and maintain safely.

In the private sector, the Organization of Socialized and Economic Housing Developers of the Philippines (OSHDP) has long been a key player in addressing the country’s housing shortage. Its members develop projects aimed at lower and middle income families, working within government regulations on affordability, land use, financing, and construction standards.

Beyond building houses, OSHDP serves as an industry voice in engaging government agencies on policies affecting home ownership. Its role has become increasingly important as the public sector pushes for larger-scale housing programs – with developers facing the difficult task of keeping homes affordable while dealing with rising labor, land, materials, funding, and compliance costs.

Last month, OSHDP held its Affordable Housing Summit at the Fairmont Hotel Makati with the theme, “Building through Uncertainty: Restoring Confidence and Stability.” The conference brought together developers, government officials, finance professionals, and technology providers to examine the pressures confronting the housing industry.

Department of Finance (DOF) Undersecretary Michael Peter Alejandro delivered the keynote address on behalf of DOF Secretary Frederick Go, whose central message was that reducing housing costs requires stronger reforms, simpler government processes, and closer public-private cooperation to expand affordable housing. Other officials who delivered messages were Senator Joseph Victor Ejercito, Valenzuela Congressman Kenneth Gatchalian, and Makati City Councilor Bernadette Sese.

Under Republic Act 7279 signed by then President Corazon Aquino in 1992, subdivision developers are required to provide socialized housing equivalent to at least 20 percent of the total subdivision area or total project cost, subject to conditions of the Balanced Housing Development Program (BHDP). This was substantially strengthened by the BHDP amendments under Republic Act 10884, which lapsed into law in 2016.

Congress is currently proposing reforms to the amended law through the House of Representatives’ recently approved House Bill 9697, which is now poised for Senate consideration. Its proposed changes to the BHDP include new compliance mechanisms and measures intended to bolster socialized housing delivery – presenting an opportunity to rethink the BHDP not merely as a regulatory obligation, but a platform to mobilize land, private capital, expertise, and completed housing toward a national objective.
Shift to horizontal housing

Among the developers that are active in affordable housing is the Century Properties Group Inc., listed in the Philippine Stock Exchange as CPG. Known for its high-end vertical condominium projects such as Century City Makati, it has shifted to horizontal developments as majority of its vertical inventory had already been sold.

This growth model has more upside potential because of the enormous unmet demand of first-time homeowners. Besides, horizontal projects can be developed in phases, allowing developers to match construction with sales rather than committing huge capital outlays upfront to a high-rise tower.

Through its first-home brand called PHirst Residential, CPG has made affordable housing a major component of its business since it entered that segment in 2017. Its PHirst Park Homes target first-time buyers in growth corridors nationwide, with 32 master planned communities in Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bataan, Bulacan, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Quezon, Iloilo, Negros Occidental, South Cotabato, and Davao del Norte. As of 2025, it has completed more than 16,000 homes and plans to build over 13,000 additional houses.

During the first half of 2026, CPG’s consolidated revenues of P7.6 billion were steady year-on-year, while its EBITDA rose nine percent to ₱2.3 billion from the same period last year – reflecting continued operating efficiency and margin discipline across its core businesses. PHirst Residential was CPG’s principal growth engine, growing seven per cent year-on-year and contributing 73 percent of the company’s consolidated revenues.

Despite the ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, reservation sales rose 11 percent in the first six months this year – signaling resilient buyer confidence and sustained demand for CPG’s expanding portfolio in the horizontal residential sphere.

J. Albert Gamboa is a Life Member of the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX) and Associate Member of the Institute of Corporate Directors. The opinion expressed herein does not necessarily reflect the views of these institutions and the Manila Bulletin. #FinexPhils www.finex.org.ph

articles.title: Haze, possibly from Indonesia fires, reached NCR, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, says DENR-EMB
articles.summary: Parts of Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Mimaropa are affected by haze, possibly tied to the ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 12:00am

Parts of Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Mimaropa are affected by haze, possibly tied to the ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) said on Monday night.
The EMB in the National Capital Region said the air quality in 10 cities has been classified as "very unhealthy." That of Parañaque City was classified as "acutely unhealthy."
The cities classified under "very unhealthy" air quality with 150 - 200 Air Quality Index (AQI) are:

items: Quezon City (Ateneo)
Malabon
Mandaluyong
Manila
Marikina
Muntinlupa
Pasay
San Juan City
Taguig
Valenzuela

blocks.text: "The DENR-EMB is continuously monitoring air quality levels through its network of air quality monitoring stations to assess the extent and potential impacts of the haze," the bureau said.

The Quezon City government has issued an "Air Quality Advisory" for residents, especially those who belong to the vulnerable group such as children, senior citizens, pregnant women, and those with lung and heart ailments, to wear face masks.
Residents are also advised to remain indoors and, for emergency concerns, may call Helpline 122. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Lingayen placed under state of calamity
articles.summary: The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Emergency responders use a rubber boat to evacuate residents of Barangay Basing in Lingayen, Pangasinan as monsoon rains inundate low-lying and near-river communities on August 29, 2026.
Cesar Ramirez

MANILA, Philippines — The capital of Pangasinan was placed under a state of calamity yesterday as the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng caused widespread flooding and damage to the province.
Headed by Vice Gov. Mark Ronald Lambino, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (SP) approved Provincial Resolution 985-2026 during a special online session declaring Lingayen under a state of calamity.

The resolution said the weather disturbances “brought torrential rains and widespread flooding in low-lying areas of Pangasinan, resulting in severe flooding and widespread impacts on communities, infrastructure, agriculture, private properties and livelihoods.”
More than 1.2 million people have been affected, according to reports from the Department of Social Welfare and Development.
Eight local government units have also declared their own states of calamity, with the number of affected families and damage expected to rise as assessment and response operations continue.
As of Aug. 30, the monsoon and the three cyclones had caused P232.5 million in infrastructure damage, more than P649 million in agricultural damage and more than P2.1 million in livestock damage.

According to the SP, the declaration will allow the automatic price freeze on basic necessities and prime commodities under Republic Act 7581, or the Price Act, to prevent overpricing, hoarding and profiteering during the emergency period.
Aside from Lingayen, other provinces nearby also sustained significant damage due to recent weather disturbances.
At least 10 houses were damaged after a strong whirlwind tore through two villages in Burgos, Ilocos Sur on Sunday evening amid heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.

Ilocos Sur Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Officer Rhon Arquelada said the incident occurred around 6 p.m. in Barangays Manaboc and Bangbangar. Several roofs and garages were damaged while trees were uprooted by strong winds.
No injuries were reported as police and disaster response teams immediately rushed to the affected areas after barangay officials alerted authorities through handheld radios.
Pampanga Gov. Lilia Pineda, meanwhile, appealed yesterday to the private sector to help in implementing projects that could address widespread flooding in their province.
“We need the participation of the private sector because the DPWH already has a lot on its plate,” she said in an interview with “Storycon” on One News.

“This is the first time that even towns that previously did not experience flooding have been submerged. The volume of water was different this time… We did not expect it. Before, we could still cope…but this time, it has really been difficult,” she added. — With Mark Ernest Villeza, Rainier Allan Ronda, Artemio Dumlao, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Congressman hits OVP execs
articles.summary: A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President as issues surrounding its use of confidential…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Gina Acosta and Lemuel Ortonio
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — A leader in the House of Representatives has pointed to a possible staffing problem and accountability failure inside the Office of the Vice President (OVP) as issues surrounding its use of confidential funds continue to unravel before the Senate impeachment court.
Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V cited the repeated claims by OVP officials that they could not remember or did not know crucial details of the confidential funds used by the office.
“Maybe they had problem with HR because they seemed to have forgotten everything. They knew nothing,” he said.

Former OVP special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and OVP Assistant Secretary and assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio were both declared hostile prosecution witnesses as the impeachment court examined how confidential funds were requested, released, implemented and liquidated under Duterte.

They both testified that they did not know how the confidential funds were used and that they put their trust in Vice President Sara Duterte and her security chief Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, whom she had tasked to handle the funds.
Ortega said government personnel entrusted with public funds are expected to perform their assigned responsibilities regardless of how much trust they place in their superiors.
“It means they’re blind followers. They just release funds, unmindful of where they would end up,” Ortega said.

Acosta testified that she turned over the funds to Lachica, the former head of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group, per Duterte’s instruction, while Ortonio testified on documents and processes involving the funds but repeatedly qualified the extent of his personal knowledge.

For Ortega, the recurring inability of officials directly involved in the transactions to explain what happened after the money left their hands raises questions about whether basic staff work was performed at all.

articles.title: NOAH head: Philippines ignored 1941 flood control master plan
articles.summary: The massive flooding being experienced in Metro Manila and various areas in the country is the result of decades of failure to follow the 1941 master plan, according to a University of the…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Residents wade through floodwaters along Zapote Junction in Las Piñas on Saturday morning, Aug. 28, 2026 as the flooded road remains closed to vehicles.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — The massive flooding being experienced in Metro Manila and various areas in the country is the result of decades of failure to follow the 1941 master plan, according to a University of the Philippines expert.

UP Resilience Institute (UPRI) executive director and Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards) head Mahar Lagmay warned Monday that flooding would continue to worsen if the country fails to implement science-based solutions.

“Our problem today is the accumulation of decades because the master plan was drafted in 1941. This is not different from the master plan of Cebu, which was the development plan of 1939 but it was not followed. The master plan would have been good, if we had followed that,” Lagmay said over radio dzBB.
“It’s all too late, the plan is to propose solutions other than just dikes, so not just one but many, let’s not call it flood control, but flood management instead,” he added.

Lagmay said concerned government agencies such as the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) are now consulting Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards) before undertaking flood-related projects.

“We have simulations that are very, very high, high-resolution. Simulations that are being done, which are constantly being passed by the DPWH, the MMDA, the designs, particularly DPWH, so that before we invest in the project, we have already seen on the computer how high the flood has been lowered, which ones will no longer be flooded…which ones would be flooded, how effective is the investment before we spend money on an area,” Lagmay said.
Since 2012, Lagmay said Project NOAH has helped reduce the number of deaths caused by floods and storms to about 250 to 300 per year.
Lagmay stressed that there is no overnight solution to the country’s flooding problem, saying authorities must begin implementing long-term measures as Metro Manila’s population continues to grow.

“This has been going on for a long time. I said 1941, that’s a few decades. We’ve been neglecting it for more than half a century, let’s not expect a magic bullet that will solve it immediately, it won’t happen tomorrow,” he said. “But it’s important to start this so that it doesn’t get worse.” — Ramon Efren Lazaro

articles.title: Study: 2 of 5 Pinoys age 10 face parental violence
articles.summary: A study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that nearly two in five Filipino children aged 10 reported physical or emotional violence from a parent.

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — A study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that nearly two in five Filipino children aged 10 reported physical or emotional violence from a parent.

“Home Should Be Safe: How Parental Violence Affects Children’s Education in the Philippines,” authored by Aaron Carlos Manuel, Lyle Daryll Casas and Valerie Gilbert Ulep, said by age 14, children exposed to parental violence were significantly less likely to be enrolled in school, particularly girls.
The authors added that exposure to parental violence at age 10 was associated with lower odds of school enrolment at age 14 among both boys and girls.
The study said the association was stronger among girls when the results were stratified by gender.
The authors said parental violence was also associated with poorer academic performance, although this relationship was not statistically significant.

Among the recommendations of the study is to sustain and scale up multisectoral early intervention programs nationwide that integrate parenting education, school-based violence prevention and community advocacy, with gender-responsive approaches tailored to the distinct needs of boys and girls.
The study was done with support from the Australian government and the United Nations Population Fund.
It noted that the burden is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where legal protections and enforcement mechanisms are often weaker.
The authors noted that despite the magnitude of the problem, policy responses in many LMICs remain inadequate.
The study said this is frequently attributed to competing resource demands and a lack of context-specific evidence on effective prevention strategies and mitigation of long-term impacts.
It added that the failure to address this issue carries substantial costs.
According to the authors, worldwide, violence against children imposes a significant economic burden due to losses in health, education and productivity.
The authors said the Philippines confronts particularly acute challenges, citing data where about eight in 10 Filipino children have experienced some form of violence.
The study said more recent data indicate six in 10 children are subjected to violent discipline at home.

The authors added that violence also extends beyond the household, saying nearly three in 10 Filipino learners reported being bullied, citing results from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s “Program for International Student Assessment 2022,” contributing to the country’s continued characterization as the “bullying capital of the world.”
Families are first line of defense

Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday said families are the first line of defense against school threats and violence, as he asked parents to be active partners in learner protection, values formation and anti-bullying efforts.
“We cannot solve violence in schools if we only act within the classroom. Home is our first defense,” Angara said.
He said families should take an active role in daily learner life and maintain close communication with school authorities.

“Let’s talk to our children every day, let’s listen to what they are going through and let’s communicate with their teachers and schools. We need to learn to notice red flags and changes in a child’s behavior before it even reaches the point of harm or bullying. Let’s make them feel that they are not alone,” Angara added.

The Department of Education issued DepEd Memorandum 002, s. 2026, or the Kaagapay Program, alongside with the Parent Effectiveness Service (PES) Program under Republic Act 11908 amid increase in school violence.

Angara said the Kaagapay Program equips parent communities with practical tools through capacity-building sessions to identify red flags, manage behavioral issues and directly coordinate with school Child Protection Committees and guidance personnel.

He said DepEd is collaborating with the Department of Social Welfare and Development to harmonize the PES modules with the Kaagapay Program, targeting full-scale implementation to tackle root causes of violence, including mental health struggles and online safety risks.

DepEd said it will roll out its program on Strengthening Collaboration of Parents and Teachers on Learner Protection across regions, including the Cordillera Administrative Region, Metro Manila, Region 2, Region 3, Region 4-A, Region 4-B and Region 5.

It said the initiative utilizes session guides developed by the DepEd Bureau of Learner Support Services-Learner Rights and Protection Division in partnership with ChildFund Philippines, Stairway Foundation Inc. and Meta Philippines.

articles.title: 3 humanitarians named 2026 Magsaysay awardees
articles.summary: Three international humanitarians were recognized on Monday by the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation for their contributions to nation building, education, health care and human rights.

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Recipients of Asia’s premier prize and highest honor were Runa Khan from Bangladesh, Tommy Koh from Singapore and Bo Kyi from Myanmar.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Three international humanitarians were recognized on Monday by the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation (RMAF) for their contributions to nation building, education, health care and human rights.

“What is emulated in the three awardees and what brings them together is greatness of spirit. All these three awardees bring solutions to certain problems,” RMAF president Susan Afan said. “These people are chosen because of their inspirational stories.”
Khan, sole 2026 female awardee, was recognized for establishing Friendship, a nongovernmental organization that provides a three-tier health system from primary to specialist care in communities.

Through her leadership, Khan expanded Friendship’s capacity to serve communities affected by climate-related challenges with “movable schools for climate migrants” that can be dismantled in hours and rebuilt when erosion threatens areas.
Koh, a diplomat, was recognized for his “steadfast faith in dialogue, the rule of law and international cooperation.”

RMAF cited Koh’s role in the negotiations among 150 nations in the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea in 1982, paving the way for the adoption of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Bo Kyi, a former political prisoner, was cited for his commitment to the “pursuit of truth, accountability and justice.”
Kyi was detained for seven years after Myanmar’s pro-democracy demonstrations in 1988.
He fled to the Thai border to evade rearrest and co-founded the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners in 2000.
Since the 2021 military coup in Myanmar, the organization has provided support and advocacy for victims of arbitrary arrest, political imprisonment and violence.
“I dedicate this award to the Burmese people fighting injustice, especially the political prisoners who continue to stand strong behind bars,” Kyi said in his acceptance speech.

“If we continue to work together in solidarity to secure the release of all political prisoners, including Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, I believe we can build a Burma that brings peace, prosperity and stability to its people and the region,” he added.
The three new laureates join the long list of Ramon Magsaysay Awardees in its 68th year, bringing the total to 359.

articles.title: Pinoys urged: Stand firm vs all forms of pressures
articles.summary: President Marcos called on Filipinos to take part in protecting national interests, counter disinformation and “stand firm against all forms of pressures” as the nation commemorated…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos called on Filipinos to take part in protecting national interests, counter disinformation and “stand firm against all forms of pressures” as the nation commemorated National Heroes’ Day yesterday.
Marcos led the wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani at Fort Bonifacio in Taguig City.

Joining Marcos were Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro, Armed Forces vice chief Lt. Gen. Rommel Roldan, National Historical Commission of the Philippines chairman Regalado Trota Jose Jr., Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Speaker Faustino Dy III.
In his speech, the President emphasized the need to educate young Filipinos about the country’s maritime rights and responsible public discourse.
He also underscored the importance of providing strong support to Filipino fishermen, whose continued presence in Philippine waters “reinforces the country’s connection to its maritime territory.”
“This is especially meaningful as we confront the challenges before our nation today,” the Chief Executive said.

“In my recent State of the Nation Address, I reaffirmed that our duty to the people extends to protecting the country’s interests, upholding the rule of law and securing the resources upon which our communities depend,” he said.

Marcos stressed the significance of the commemoration of National Heroes’ Day as the nation marked the 10th anniversary this year of the 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ maritime entitlements under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea or UNCLOS.
“We will fight for our rights through peaceful means, in accordance with the law and consistent with our principles,” he said.
Marcos reiterated that defending the country’s territory is a responsibility shared by the entire nation.

“It calls on each of us to understand our history, to know our rights and to take part in protecting the national interests. We begin by educating the youth on where our maritime rights come from and why they matter,” he said.
Marcos likewise urged the public to champion truth, counter disinformation and encourage responsible discourse across every platform available to them.
He also reminded Filipinos of their collective duty to uphold the integrity of institutions, by demanding transparency, accountability and a level of governance the nation truly deserves.

“Together, let us shape a Bagong Pilipinas whose people stand firm against all forms of pressures, where institutions serve with integrity and where sovereignty remains secure for generations to come,” Marcos said.
Modern-day heroes
Marcos also recognized ordinary Filipinos who continue to make sacrifices for their families and communities.
“But the National Heroes Day also offers an invitation to look beyond the pages of history. After all, the spirit of heroism lives on because every generation gives it a new face,” he said.
He said honor should be given to people who choose to serve, care and contribute to a cause greater than oneself.

“We see it in our soldiers and first responders who risk their lives to keep us safe. We recognize it in our teachers, health workers, farmers, fisherfolk and overseas Filipinos who sustain our families and communities,” the President said.
The Chief Executive said the occasion must go beyond remembering the nation’s heroes as he urged Filipinos to continue advancing development.

“Our forebears won our freedom, defended our dignity and laid the foundations of the Republic we cherish. We honor them best by embodying their courage, keeping the flame of patriotism alive and becoming the citizens our country needs,” he said.
National Heroes’ Day is observed every last Monday of August as a regular national holiday under Republic Act 9492.
Marcos also visited the tomb of his father and namesake at the Libingan ng mga Bayani.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, in his message, called on Filipinos and government officials alike to translate the sacrifices of the nation’s forebears into meaningful public service with honesty and compassion.
“As we honor the men and women whose sacrifices secured our freedom, sovereignty and democracy, let us remember that their legacy calls us to continue building a better nation,” he said.

Sen. Francis Pangilinan highlighted the unsung heroism of ordinary citizens, noting the coincidence of the holiday falling within the traditional Chinese ghost month. “Be reminded, true heroes don’t ‘ghost.’”

Pangilinan recognized overseas Filipino workers, environmental defenders, food producers and disaster volunteers who wade through floods during calamities to deliver relief. — Daphne Galvez, Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: DPWH fund utilization remains sluggish
articles.summary: Despite bigger cash allocations to state agencies in the first seven months of the year, spending rate turned out to be uneven during the period, with the Department of Public Works and Highways…

blocks.text: September 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Public Works and Highways.
Businessworld / File

MANILA, Philippines — Despite bigger cash allocations to state agencies in the first seven months of the year, spending rate turned out to be uneven during the period, with the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) – currently at the center of the flood control scandal – posting sluggish utilization.

Data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) showed that notices of cash allocation (NCAs) rose by 4.7 percent to P3.13 trillion as of end-July from P2.99 trillion in the same period last year.
Even with the increase, government agencies posted only slightly higher utilization rate of 94.6 percent from 94 percent in the seven-month period in 2025.
Of the total releases, P2.96 trillion had been utilized, leaving P169.94 billion unused as of end-July.

NCAs are disbursement orders by the DBM to government banks servicing the release of funds to agencies. State agencies are expected to use the NCAs to pay for the cash requirements of their programs and projects.
A higher utilization ratio indicates greater capacity of agencies to implement their programs and projects.

Line departments accounted for about 69 percent of total NCA releases, receiving P2.16 trillion. The remaining P969.11 billion was directed to other agencies, especially state-run firms and local governments.

Departments registered a utilization rate of 92.2 percent, using P1.99 trillion of the P2.16 trillion for the NCAs they received as of end-July. In the same period last year, the spending rate was only 92 percent.

The Department of Education (DepEd) received the largest NCA among line departments at P513.94 billion, followed by the DPWH with P320.13 billion. Both departments recorded lower utilization rates than a year earlier.

The DPWH utilized 86.2 percent of its NCA as of end-July, down from 94 percent a year earlier. The slower utilization comes as the agency faces heightened scrutiny over its infrastructure spending amid the flood-control controversy.
The DPWH has tightened the review, audit and validation of payment claims for infrastructure projects, as well as documentary compliance requirements for contractors.
DepEd, meanwhile, utilized 93.1 percent of its NCA, down from 97 percent a year earlier.
No line department recorded a full 100 percent utilization rate during the period.

Some of the agencies that recorded above 90 percent utilization rates were the Office of the Vice President and Commission on Audit, followed by the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Department of Energy.
The Office of the President posted the lowest utilization rate among departments and offices, using 69.4 percent of its P10.68 billion NCA, or about P7.41 billion, as of end-July.

The Presidential Communications Office had a utilization rate of 72 percent, while the Department of Labor and Employment and Department of Agriculture posted rates of 76.8 percent and 79.4 percent, respectively.
